question: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation research, how do figure- or table-based evaluations quantify model performance on the ADE20K dataset and its standard partitions?
answer: Figure-based evaluations quantify ADE20K performance through mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) scores reported in comparative tables. In 'Training-Free Class Purification for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation', the ADE20K result appears as 'ADE' in a multi-dataset comparison table, where refining activations with ground-truth vocabulary improves mIoU from 59.4 (baseline) to 72.0 — demonstrating the impact of class purification on ADE20K. In 'Effective SAM Combination for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation', Table 3 reports ADE20K performance across two standard partitions: A-847 and A-150. Using points-only yields 15.2 (A-847) and 37.8 (A-150); masks-only yields 15.1 and 38.1; and the best-performing points+masks combination achieves 18.1 (A-847) and 41.8 (A-150). Together, these figure facts show that ADE20K is leveraged both as a holistic benchmark ('ADE') and via fine-grained partitions ('A-847', 'A-150') to measure segmentation accuracy under vocabulary-aware and prompt-engineering strategies. The paper DPSeg: Dual-Prompt Cost Volume Learning for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that using visual prompt generators — LayerDiffuse, SD-V1.5, and SD-V3 — yields ADE20K mIoU scores ranging from 12.1–96.3 across evaluation settings, outperforming the text-prompt-only baseline (11.4–94.4). The paper CLIPer: Hierarchically Improving Spatial Representation of CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that early-layer attention with early-layer embeddings achieves an mIoU of 39.6 on ADE20K (reported as 'Object').

question: In papers related to Whole Slide Image Classification, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize approaches to improving computational efficiency?
answer: Paper A (HistoFS) provides quantitative, table-based evidence of computational efficiency: in Table 6, it reports that on the RCC dataset, the HistoFS method achieves a communication load of 196.77 MB and an average training time of 760 seconds per global round—both lower than the 420.00 MB and 1485 seconds required by CCST [21]. Paper B (FOCUS) offers structural, architecture-diagram-supported evidence: its framework explicitly decomposes efficiency into three complementary visual compression mechanisms—(a) knowledge-enhanced adaptive global redundancy removal using a Foundation Model and Text Encoder, (b) sequential fine-grained local redundancy removal via a filter, and (c) cross-modal aggregation with pathology knowledge prompts—thereby characterizing efficiency as a hierarchical, knowledge-guided visual token reduction process. The paper GMMamba: Group Masking Mamba for Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that the Cross-group Super-feature Sampling (CSS) module improves computational efficiency through a structured token compression pipeline: Max-Pooling yields f_s^max, which drives Cross-attention to produce f_s^ca; Multi-head Attention refines this into f_s^mha; and an Association Matrix Q combines both to generate the final compressed super-feature f_sgr.

question: In papers evaluating 3D human pose estimation, how do figure- or table-based analyses empirically ground the MPJPE metric — for instance, in method comparisons versus architectural design-space analysis?
answer: In PoseAnchor, MPJPE is grounded as a concrete performance value in Table 3: PoseAnchor achieves an MPJPE of 40.3 on the MixSTE model, directly compared against three other root position estimation methods (Baseline, Root+, ZS-anchor) — illustrating its role in method-level benchmarking. In HiPART, MPJPE is grounded as a trend-sensitive metric in a figure/table analyzing codebook dimension ablation: MPJPE improves as codebook dimension increases from 32 to 128, plateaus with diminishing returns beyond 128, and peaks at dimension 2048 (sparse tokens) and 3072 (dense tokens) on Human3.6M — illustrating its role in characterizing architectural design trade-offs. The paper Semantics-aware Test-time Adaptation for 3D Human Pose Estimation provides figure-based evidence that for the 'downtown_bar' video, the proposed method (Ours) achieves an MPJPE of 83.8 and a PA-MPJPE of 58.2, outperforming CycleAdapt (MPJPE 97.3, PA-MPJPE 65.0) and other variants.

question: In papers on camouflaged object detection, what figure- or table-based evidence demonstrates how architectural or prompting enhancements improve detection capability?
answer: Paper A provides qualitative figure-based evidence: Figure 6 shows, across five sample images, that the Adaptive Refinement Module (ARM) refines multimodal prompts such that their heatmaps become more focused and fully cover the target camouflaged object — in contrast to the initial diffuse prompts from BLIP. Paper B provides quantitative table-based evidence: Table 1 reports that SAM-DSA achieves top-ranked scores (marked in red/blue/orange) across multiple metrics (M, F^w, S_m, E^x, alphaE) on four standard COD datasets (CAMO, CHAMELEON, COD10K, NC4K), outperforming other RGB- and RGB-D-based methods including baseline SAM variants (indicated by dagger symbol). Together, these figure facts demonstrate complementary forms of empirical support — visual localization fidelity and systematic benchmark superiority — for enhanced COD capability.

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do figure-based visualizations characterize the impact of technical design choices on the spatial structure or statistical properties of intermediate diffusion signals?
answer: LUSD visualizes edit-specific gradients to show that stronger score distillation (High SD) yields more localized and intense gradients—e.g., for '+ bird' and '+ scarf' edits—indicating improved spatial focus of edit-relevant signal. SwiftEdit visualizes inverted noise to demonstrate that including the stage-2 regularization loss (Lregu^stage2) produces high-frequency, artifact-free noise resembling ideal Gaussian noise, whereas omitting it retains source-image artifacts—revealing how regularization improves statistical alignment of intermediate noise with the diffusion process assumptions. The paper Training-Free Text-Guided Image Editing with Visual Autoregressive Model provides figure-based evidence that its architecture includes an adaptive mask for fine-grained editing and a Causal VAR Transformer for caching randomness—design choices visually linked to enhanced spatial control and statistical handling of intermediate diffusion signals.

question: In papers on retrieval-augmented generation frameworks, how do figure- or table-based architectural descriptions characterize the role and implementation of entity extraction within the offline indexing or graph construction pipeline?
answer: LightRAG positions entity extraction as one module ('Entity & Rel Extraction') embedded in the 'Graph-based Text Indexing' stage — a broader phase that also includes LLM Profiling and Deduplication — indicating an integrated, multi-objective indexing strategy where entity extraction serves graph construction but is co-located with other profiling tasks. In contrast, LinearRAG treats entity extraction as a distinct, early step in the 'Offline Construction' phase, explicitly implemented using spaCy, and directly feeding into semantic linking to build a Tri-Graph — reflecting a more modular, tool-specialized, and graph-first pipeline design. These figure-based architectural depictions highlight divergent engineering trade-offs: LightRAG emphasizes lightweight synergy across indexing subtasks, whereas LinearRAG prioritizes explicit, library-backed entity identification as a prerequisite for structured graph assembly.

question: In papers addressing mitigating object hallucination in vision-language models, how do figure- or table-based empirical analyses characterize the sensitivity of mitigation performance to intervention-specific control parameters?
answer: Paper A uses Table 10 to show how MemVR’s total score varies across different visual retracing (VR) strategies—specifically reporting scores of 1896.7 (Dynamic), 1847.6 (Static-7), 1881.2 (Static-15), 1858.1 (Static-23), and 1889.2 (Static-φ)—demonstrating that performance is sensitive to the choice of VR strategy as a controllable intervention parameter. Paper B presents a line chart showing how the F1 score for object hallucination detection changes with the hyperparameter alpha: for LLaVA-v1.5, F1 peaks at ~85.5 near alpha = 50 then declines; for Qwen-VL, F1 peaks at ~83.0 at the same alpha value—indicating that mitigation efficacy is non-monotonic and highly sensitive to alpha tuning. Together, these figure-based analyses contrast two distinct approaches to parameterizing and empirically evaluating intervention sensitivity: one via discrete strategy comparison (table of aggregate scores), the other via continuous hyperparameter sweep (curve of fine-grained metric). The paper Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Image-Grounded Guidance provides figure-based evidence that Figure 3 contains three line charts showing the effect of guidance strength (γ) on CHAIR metrics for LLaVA, LLaVA-v1.5, and mPLUG-Owl2: as γ increases from 0 to 1, the CHAIRs score for LLaVA decreases from approximately 0.25 to 0.15, while the Recall score increases from 0.40 to 0.50.

question: In papers on zero-shot composed image retrieval, how do figure- or table-based empirical results quantify the R@1 retrieval performance of the ViT-L/14 backbone?
answer: The paper 'Missing Target-Relevant Information Prediction with World Model...' reports that, on the CIRR dataset, PrediCIR with a ViT-L/14 backbone achieves an R1 score of 27.2. Meanwhile, 'Reason-before-Retrieve: One-Stage Reflective Chain-of-Thoughts...' reports that, on the GeneCIS test data under the 'Change Object' task, the OSrCIR method with a ViT-L/14 backbone achieves an R@1 score of 16.1. These values reflect ViT-L/14’s empirically observed retrieval accuracy in distinct zero-shot compositional settings, as captured in their respective evaluation tables or result figures. The paper Generative Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that Table 7a shows the 'Pseudo token' fusion strategy achieves a RecallSubset@K score of 89.45 at K=3 on the CIRR validation set. The paper Hierarchy-Aware Pseudo Word Learning with Text Adaptation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that, on the CIRR and FashionIQ datasets, the HIT model with a ViT-L/14 backbone achieves R@1 scores of 37.3 and 34.5, respectively, when using all three token types. The paper Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Dual-Stream Instruction-Aware Distillation provides figure-based evidence that, on the GeneCIS test set under the 'Change Object' task, DistillCIR with a ViT-L/14 backbone achieves an R@1 score of 17.34.

question: In papers on federated instruction tuning, how do figure- or table-based descriptions characterize the multi-stage procedural architecture used to address data heterogeneity across clients?
answer: The paper 'Optimizing Cross-Client Domain Coverage for Federated Instruction Tuning of Large Language Models' describes a three-stage process for FedDCA: (1) client-side clustering with cluster center upload, (2) server-side augmentation via diversity-oriented client center selection and data retrieval, and (3) collaborative fine-tuning through LoRA parameter exchange between clients and server. In contrast, 'FedDQC: Data Quality Control in Federated Instruction-tuning of Large Language Models' presents a two-stage architecture: Stage 1 (Scoring Stage) uses the global model to compute Instruction-Response Alignment (IRA) scores per local sample and selects high-scoring subsets; Stage 2 (Hierarchical Training Stage) trains the global model iteratively over hierarchically aggregated high-quality subsets from clients. Together, these figure-based procedural descriptions illustrate divergent architectural priorities—diversity-driven data coverage versus alignment-driven data quality—in federated instruction tuning system design.

question: In papers on automated red teaming of text-to-image models, how do figure- or table-based analyses quantify and visualize attack success rate across multiple target models?
answer: Paper A (AutoPrompt) uses Table 4 to report static transferability of adversarial prompts across four safe T2I models: ESD (100% success), SLD-MAX (59.35%), Receler (41.46%), and AdvUnlearn (9.76%), along with reverse transfer rates (e.g., ESD-generated prompts achieve 43.97% success on SLD-MAX). Paper B (Automated Red Teaming via Feedback-Guided Iteration) uses Figure 3 to show dynamic convergence of attack success rate over iterative rounds, demonstrating that Stable Diffusion 1.5, 2.1, XL, FLUX.1-dev, and DeepFloyd IF all reach near-perfect success (~1.0) after 10 rounds. Together, these figure facts illustrate two complementary empirical approaches to measuring red-teaming efficacy: cross-model transferability versus within-model iterative convergence.

question: In papers on weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do figure- or table-based fine-grained evaluations quantify overall localization performance using average mean Average Precision (AVG mAP)?
answer: The paper 'Learning Event Completeness for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection' reports an AVG mAP of 13.56 on UCF-Crime, computed from mAP@IoU scores across IoU thresholds 0.1–0.5 (19.65, 17.17, 14.37, 9.45, 7.18). The paper 'CMHKF: Cross-Modality Heterogeneous Knowledge Fusion for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection' reports an AVG mAP of 26.70% on XD-Violence, stated as the highest value in its fine-grained comparison table — with 'Ours(light)' achieving 24.86% as the second-best result. Both values are explicitly extracted from fine-grained evaluation tables that aggregate localization performance across IoU thresholds.

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do qualitative result grids visually structure and juxtapose editing tasks and outputs to demonstrate model capability across diverse text instructions and input images?
answer: Paper A (LUSD) organizes its qualitative results grid by editing prompt — showing nine distinct text prompts (e.g., '+ stylish sunglasses', 'a lake of lava', 'a cat with blue eyes') applied to a shared set of input images, with each column corresponding to a method (including 'Ours') to enable cross-method comparison per prompt. Paper B (Training-Free Text-Guided Image Editing) organizes its visual results by input image transformation — displaying rows where each row starts from a single original image (e.g., a goat, a rabbit, a car) and shows multiple edited versions reflecting different text-guided changes (e.g., 'goat → horse', 'rabbit → cat', 'car → motorcycle', 'makeup gold → blue'), emphasizing input-specific versatility and output diversity within a single task context.

question: In papers related to mathematical reasoning, how do figure- or table-based empirical results characterize the impact of model training interventions on accuracy across benchmark datasets?
answer: Paper A (CogAtom) reports figure-based trends showing that increasing the scale of synthesized training data—from +300k to +1.6M samples—leads to consistent accuracy gains across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks: GSM8K (+1.5 percentage points, from 90.1% to 91.6%), MATH (+3.4 pp, 87.2% → 90.6%), AIME (+6.0 pp, 27.0% → 33.0%), and AMC (+4.8 pp, 59.4% → 64.2%). Paper B (ClozeMath) presents table-based results demonstrating that adopting a cloze-style equation-filling objective improves GSM8K accuracy relative to standard fine-tuning (MFT) across four LLMs: +2.10 pp for DeepSeek-Math (77.10 vs. MFT baseline), +1.97 pp for Llama-3.1-8B (75.97), +2.39 pp for Llama-3.2-3B (57.39), and +1.84 pp for Llama-3.2-1B (31.84). Together, these illustrate contrasting yet complementary intervention strategies—data scaling versus objective redesign—each empirically validated via benchmark accuracy measurements in figures or tables. The paper Safe: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via Retrospective Step-aware Formal Verification provides figure-based evidence that the Safe (Ours) intervention improves MATH accuracy over the LSTM (Ours) baseline—achieving 80.4 vs. 78.9 for GPT-4o, and 52.4 vs. 48.2 for Deepseek-Math. The paper Chain-of-Reasoning: Towards Unified Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via a Multi-Paradigm Perspective provides figure-based evidence that adopting a multi-paradigm chain-of-reasoning (CoR) training strategy improves MATH and GSM8K accuracy across model scales: Qwen2.5-Math (CoR) 7B achieves 64.7 on MATH and 90.0 on GSM8K—outperforming its 1.5B variant—and Llama-3.1 (CoR) 70B achieves 70.7 on MATH and 90.0 on GSM8K—outperforming its 8B variant. The paper GRPO-LEAD: A Difficulty-Aware Reinforcement Learning Approach for Concise Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models provides figure-based evidence that the LEAD-stage2 intervention achieves a Cons@32 score of 0.867 and a Pass@1 score of 0.650 on the AIME24 benchmark, and a Cons@32 score of 0.767 and a Pass@1 score of 0.539 on the AIME25 benchmark.

question: In papers on biomedical entity linking, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize top-1 accuracy on the NCBI dataset across different modeling strategies?
answer: Paper A reports that the ANGEL model achieves 92.8 top-1 accuracy on the NCBI dataset, outperforming GenBioEL (91.0); this reflects a generative entity linking approach trained with negative samples. Paper B reports that the Llama-3-8b model, guided by restrictive and contrastive decoding, achieves peak Hits@1 of ~93% on NCBI when retrieving k=2 candidate entities — higher than its performance at larger k values — and further shows that 10-shot prompting consistently improves performance over zero-shot prompting across k. Together, these figure-based results illustrate how top-1 accuracy on NCBI varies with architectural paradigm (generative vs. LLM-decoding), retrieval scope (k), and prompting strategy (shot count).

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, what do figure- or table-based analyses reveal about how cross-modal representation fusion contributes to both anomaly detection performance and semantic separation of anomaly classes?
answer: The two papers jointly demonstrate that cross-modal fusion improves both quantitative detection performance and qualitative feature discriminability. In 'Learning Event Completeness for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection', ablation results (Fact A) show that including the cross-modal branch (CMB) boosts AVG mAP@IoU from 30.17 (vision-only) to 34.94 (full model), indicating measurable performance gains attributable to cross-modal integration. In 'CMHKF: Cross-Modality Heterogeneous Knowledge Fusion for Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection', t-SNE visualization (Fact B) on the XD-Violence dataset reveals that CMHKF features yield tighter, more separable clusters for distinct anomaly classes (e.g., Abuse, Explosion, Shooting) compared to overlapping Pretrained CLIP Features — providing direct visual evidence that cross-modal fusion enhances semantic discriminability in latent space. Together, these figure-based findings synthesize a coherent insight: cross-modal representation fusion strengthens weakly-supervised video anomaly detection not only through higher mAP but also by structuring the feature space to better distinguish fine-grained anomaly semantics. The paper Just Dance with pi! A Poly-modal Inductor for Weakly-supervised Video Anomaly Detection provides figure-based evidence that in the class-wise AUC comparison on the UCF-Crime dataset, the π-VAD model consistently achieves higher scores than the UR-DMU baseline across all anomaly classes — e.g., 0.81 vs. 0.69 for 'Abuse', 0.70 vs. 0.65 for 'Arson', and 0.91 vs. 0.79 for 'Robbery'. The paper Mixture of Experts Guided by Gaussian Splatters Matters: A new Approach to Weakly-Supervised Video Anomaly Detection provides figure-based evidence that the combination of TGS, MoE, and Gate in the GS-MoE framework achieves 91.58% AUC on UCF-Crime and 94.52% AUC on XD-Violence, along with 51.63% AP_A on UCF-Crime and 85.74% AP_A on XD-Violence — demonstrating how its cross-modal component integration boosts quantitative anomaly detection performance.

question: In fake news detection research, how do figure- or table-based ablation studies characterize the performance contribution of individual model components when evaluated on the GossipCop dataset?
answer: The DCCF framework (Disentangling Fact from Sentiment) reports that removing the 'w/o Evolution' component causes accuracy to drop from 0.904 (full model) to 0.879 on GossipCop—a 2.5-point absolute decrease—demonstrating the importance of its dynamic evolution mechanism. In contrast, ZoFia (Zero-Shot Fake News Detection) reports that removing the debate component reduces the F1-score from 61.2 to 59.2 on GossipCop (a 2.0-point drop), while removing expert analysis causes a larger decline to 57.3 (a 3.9-point drop), highlighting the differential sensitivity of zero-shot reasoning to analytical and interactive components. Both studies use ablation on GossipCop to empirically isolate component-level contributions, but differ in metric (accuracy vs. F1), granularity (single-component removal vs. combinatorial removals), and functional focus (dynamic multimodal evolution vs. retrieval-guided multi-LLM interaction).

question: In papers on training-free zero-shot composed image retrieval, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize method performance on the CIRCO benchmark when using the ViT-B/32 backbone?
answer: The OSrCIR method (Reason-before-Retrieve paper) achieves a mAP@25 score of 20.94 on the CIRCO + CIRR test data with ViT-B/32. In contrast, CoTMR (CoTMR paper) reports a mAP@10 score of 22.78 on the CIRCO benchmark alone using the same ViT-B/32 backbone — the highest result for that setting in Table 2. Both results are derived from quantitative evaluations in figures or tables and reflect distinct but comparable instantiations of performance under the shared CIRCO + ViT-B/32 evaluation protocol. The paper Hierarchy-Aware Pseudo Word Learning with Text Adaptation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that the proposed HIT method with a BLIP ViT-L/16 backbone achieves a mAP@25 score of 21.8 on the CIRCO test set. The paper Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Dual-Stream Instruction-Aware Distillation provides figure-based evidence that, under feature distillation ablations with ViT-B/32 as the student backbone, using a LLaVA-Phi3 teacher yields a CIRR R@1 of 33.79, and using a LLaVA-LLaMA3 teacher for direct CIR yields a CIRR R@1 of 34.17.

question: In papers on Next POI Recommendation, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the representation of geographic or behavioral structure?
answer: In 'Efficient Model-Agnostic Continual Learning for Next POI Recommendation', Table IV quantitatively characterizes model behavior through accuracy and ranking metrics (Acc@5, Acc@10, Acc@20, MRR) across five temporal data blocks on the CA dataset — revealing how well models retain and generalize geographic-behavioral patterns over time under continual learning. In 'Knowledge Graph Tokenization for Behavior-Aware Generative Next POI Recommendation', the scatter plot of SIDs (Session ID embeddings) on the FB dataset visually demonstrates weak geographic coherence: circles representing POIs from the same region are scattered without forming clear clusters, indicating limited implicit encoding of regional structure in the learned embeddings. Together, these figure-based findings jointly ground the evaluation of geographic/behavioral representation — one via structured performance metrics tied to temporal dynamics, the other via spatial distribution patterns in embedding space. The paper Refine-POI: Reinforcement Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that the performance of Refine-POI on the NYC dataset is as follows: Acc@1 is 0.3469, Acc@5 is 0.5984, Acc@10 is 0.6627, and MRR is 0.4520. Its variants, Refine-POI-len and Refine-POI-guide, show lower performance across all these metrics. The paper Context-Adaptive Graph Neural Networks for Next POI Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that on the PHO dataset, the CAGNN model achieves HR@1 = 0.2945***, HR@5 = 0.5611**, HR@10 = 0.6271**, N@1 = 0.2945***, N@5 = 0.4347***, and N@10 = 0.4566*** — representing improvements of 16.82%, 7.55%, 5.64%, 16.82%, 14.21%, and 10.66% over the best baseline, thereby offering a new table-based characterization of behavioral consistency and geographic-aware ranking performance.

question: In papers on 3D human pose estimation, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize approaches to keypoint generation, refinement, or quality control?
answer: The MV-SSM paper uses an architecture diagram to show that keypoint generation relies on a ResNet-50 backbone followed by stacked Projective State Space (PSS) Blocks—each containing an SS2D Block, normalization, and feed-forward network with residual connections—and culminates in geometric triangulation to produce 3D keypoints. In contrast, the Semantics-aware Test-time Adaptation paper uses a bar chart to empirically demonstrate a trade-off in keypoint quality control: increasing the fill-in threshold from 0.55 to 0.80 reduces the ratio of filled-in keypoints (blue bars) while improving the 2D PCK score (green bars), revealing how confidence-based filtering affects both completeness and accuracy of intermediate 2D keypoint estimates used in 3D reconstruction. The paper PoseAnchor: Robust Root Position Estimation for 3D Human Pose Estimation provides figure-based evidence that Table 4 shows PoseAnchor achieves lower Abs-MPJPE (366.2) than Root+ (524.7) at high input noise (σ = 10), demonstrating improved robustness in keypoint refinement under perturbed 2D inputs.

question: In studies of attack transferability against text-to-image models, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize the variation in attack success rates across different target models?
answer: Figure-based evaluations quantify attack transferability as success rates across target models: Paper A (Table 7) reports that attacks generated on SD 1.5 achieve 100.0% success on SD 1.5 itself, but drop to 72.79% on SD 2.1, 78.10% on SD XL, and 87.17% on FLUX.1 [dev], indicating strong but non-uniform transfer across foundational diffusion models. Paper B (Table 4) shows markedly lower and more heterogeneous transfer for LLM-generated prompts: the P4D-N method achieves 100% on ESD but only 59.35% on SLD-MAX, 41.46% on Receler, and just 9.76% on AdvUnlearn — suggesting sharply diminished transfer against aggressively safety-aligned models. Together, these table-based results empirically demonstrate that transferability is highly dependent on both the source attack methodology and the architectural/safety characteristics of the target models. The paper Ferret: Faster and Effective Automated Red Teaming with Reward-Based Scoring Technique provides figure-based evidence that FERRET (RM) achieves a 0.95 average Attack Success Rate on Llama 2-chat 7B (evaluated with Llama Guard 2), outperforming RAINBOW TEAMING + CF (0.89) and RAINBOW TEAMING default (0.49); similarly, it achieves 0.95 ASR on GPT-4, compared to 0.81 and 0.92 for the same baselines.

question: In papers on GUI grounding, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the technical approaches used to achieve precise localization of UI elements in response to language queries?
answer: R-VLM introduces a region-aware training objective where precise localization is enabled through an efficient IoU-aware weighted cross-entropy computation involving three concrete steps: (a) generating M pseudo bounding boxes from the ground-truth box, (b) masking the attention map to prevent pseudo boxes from attending to each other, and (c) modifying the position embedding to ensure a single prediction at inference time. DiMo-GUI complements this by empirically validating grounding components via ablation: for the OS-Atlas-7B model, dynamic grounding alone improves the performance score from 18.4 (vanilla) to 45.7, while the full DiMo-GUI framework—including modality-aware visual reasoning—achieves 49.7, demonstrating how modular design choices quantitatively impact localization fidelity. Together, these figure-based analyses show that precise GUI grounding relies both on geometrically informed loss design and empirically validated modality-aware reasoning pathways.

question: In papers on demonstration selection for in-context learning, how do figures or tables quantitatively evaluate the quality of selected demonstrations?
answer: Paper A uses Table 1 to quantitatively evaluate demonstration selection quality via task accuracy scores (e.g., 79.91 on GSM8K with GPT-3.5-turbo for CASE; 95.92 on StrategyQA with GPT-4o-mini for CASE), comparing multiple methods across five reasoning-heavy datasets. Paper B uses Figure 2a and 2b to quantify selection quality via regression-style metrics: Figure 2a shows Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) decreasing as k increases (20–30) in both linear and non-linear settings, and Figure 2b shows that the proposed method ('Ours') achieves lower Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the query than baselines ('Top-k', 'Random-k') across the same k range — directly linking selection strategy to predictive fidelity on the target query. The paper Let The Jury Decide: Fair Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning through Incremental Greedy Evaluation provides figure-based evidence that for the Adult dataset, as the jury size increases from 1 to 100, the accuracy metric increases from approximately 0.55 to a plateau near 0.75, while the ΔDP metric decreases from approximately 0.25 to below 0.10. The paper Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning via Reinforcement Learning provides figure-based evidence that in the performance comparison on closed-source LLMs (Table 1), for the BANKING77 dataset using the GPT-3.5-turbo model, the RDES/C method achieved a score of 0.858, while the RDES/B method scored 0.767. For the CLINC150 dataset with the same model, RDES/C scored 0.949 and RDES/B scored 0.845.

question: In papers on camouflaged object detection, how do figure- or table-based analyses jointly characterize detection quality in terms of foreground-scale robustness and object boundary fidelity?
answer: UCOD-DPL provides figure-based evidence of foreground-scale robustness: on the COD10K-Test dataset, its performance charts show that the proposed method maintains high S-measure, E-measure, and F-measure across all foreground ratios — especially excelling at smaller ratios where competing methods degrade — indicating strong localization completeness under scale variation. ESCNet contributes complementary figure-based evidence of boundary fidelity: in visual comparisons on boundary-dense images, its 'Ours' segmentation masks exhibit more complete and accurate object boundaries than ground truth and six state-of-the-art methods (CamoFormer, FEDER, FSPNet, SegMaR, ZoomNet), demonstrating superior fine-grained contour recovery despite camouflage. Together, these figure facts illustrate a dual emphasis on scale-invariant detection capability and precise boundary delineation as key empirical strengths in recent camouflaged object detection approaches. The paper Enhancing Prompt Generation with Adaptive Refinement for Camouflaged Object Detection provides figure-based evidence that Figure 4 displays six charts comparing the performance of the proposed method ('Ours') with five other SOTA methods on CHAMELEON, CAMO, and COD10K, where its red solid line consistently ranks at or near the top in both Fβ versus threshold and Precision-Recall curves — indicating robust detection reliability across varying decision thresholds and recall levels, supporting both foreground-scale adaptability and boundary-sensitive precision-recall balance. The paper Improving SAM for Camouflaged Object Detection via Dual Stream Adapters provides figure-based evidence that the attentional visualization of dual-stream inputs shows the effect of adding modules incrementally: starting from the base adapter, subsequent rows show the visual attention maps when adding BKD (Bidirectional Knowledge Distillation) and MPE (Mixed Prompt Embedding) modules for both RGB and Depth inputs, illustrating how attention focus progressively refines toward object boundaries and scale-invariant regions.

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do figure- or table-based analyses empirically characterize the preservation of visual content during editing?
answer: The paper 'Training-Free Text-Guided Image Editing with Visual Autoregressive Model' uses an ablation study to show that hyperparameter gamma controls preservation of low-frequency details (e.g., global structure and background layout), while tau governs preservation of high-frequency details (e.g., textures and fine edges), with specific visual outcomes demonstrated across parameter combinations. Meanwhile, 'LUSD: Localized Update Score Distillation' reports human evaluation results quantifying preservation along four perceptual dimensions: users preferred alternative methods over LUSD 33.5% of the time for 'Background' preservation, 40.0% for 'Prompt' fidelity, 36.5% for 'Quality' of edited elements, and 36.0% overall — revealing systematic trade-offs in preservation that align with the low- vs. high-frequency control axis identified in the first paper. The paper LOCATEdit: Graph Laplacian Optimized Cross Attention for Localized Text-Guided Image Editing provides figure-based evidence that in Table 1, qualitative comparisons show that for the prompt 'an orange black cat sitting on top of a fence', LOCATEEdit produces an edited image where the cat is changed to black, while other methods like ViMAEdit, InfEdit, MasaCtrl, and LEDITS++ produce different or less accurate results.

question: In research on GUI grounding, how do figure- or table-based representations characterize the structural organization of grounding systems — whether as data generation pipelines or as domain-structured benchmark collections?
answer: Paper A's pipeline diagram characterizes GUI grounding as a three-stage data generation workflow: (1) GUI trajectory collecting via crawler (Web) or Android Emulator (Mobile), (2) Autonomous Functionality Annotation with Rejection, Annotation, and Verification modules that compare UI state changes pre- and post-interaction, and (3) formatting (Screenshot, Element, Functionality) triplets into instruction-following training data. Paper B's category breakdown table characterizes GUI grounding as a domain-structured benchmark: WinSpot organizes tasks into four application groups — File Management (16.3%), System Settings (7.1%), Productivity Tools (12.2%), and MS Store & Web (9.2%) — populated with concrete Windows applications including Windows Explorer, Task Manager, Device Manager, Disk Management, Event Viewer, Microsoft Word, Outlook, Teams, Settings App, Windows Terminal, Command Prompt, Snipping Tool, Microsoft Store, and Web browsers. The paper DiMo-GUI: Advancing Test-time Scaling in GUI Grounding via Modality-Aware Visual Reasoning provides figure-based evidence that GUI grounding can be structured as a three-stage test-time visual reasoning pipeline: (1) 'Divide Modalities,' separating text and icon elements; (2) 'Dynamic Zooming,' iteratively refining the target region via cropping; and (3) 'Select Answer,' choosing between text- and icon-based candidates based on the instruction. The paper UI-E2I-Synth: Advancing GUI Grounding with Large-Scale Instruction Synthesis provides figure-based evidence that the proposed UI-E2I-Synth pipeline is structured into three sequential steps: Step 1 involves Raw Data Collection and Parsing to generate a Heuristic Parser and Screenshot; Step 2 is Referring Expression (RE) Generation, which produces an Element Candidates Pool and an Element RE Pool containing both explicit and implicit expressions; Step 3 is Instruction Synthesis, which uses User Action Parameters to generate the final User Instruction.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do figures characterize model output behavior in relation to anomalous events?
answer: Figures characterize model output behavior in complementary ways: Paper A's visualization shows temporal class-score dynamics — for 'Shooting' and 'Fighting' events, the corresponding class detection scores (red and blue lines) peak sharply within their ground truth intervals, while the 'normal' class score (green line) remains high outside those intervals — demonstrating event-localized discriminative capability. Paper B's visualization characterizes output behavior through modality-wise performance attribution: on UCF-Crime, the five-modality fusion ('Pose + Depth + Text + Pan. Mask + Motion') achieves the highest AUC (solid green line), whereas 'RGB Only' yields consistently lower AUC (dotted red line), revealing how input modality composition governs overall discriminative capacity under weak supervision. The paper Mixture of Experts Guided by Gaussian Splatters Matters: A new Approach to Weakly-Supervised Video Anomaly Detection provides figure-based evidence that for the 'Arson-011' video, the Gaussian splatter creates a long distribution over the temporal axis, while for the 'Assault-010' video, it creates a small variance around two detected peaks.

question: In papers on 3D semantic scene completion, how do qualitative figure-based evaluations characterize the visual fidelity of completed scenes in terms of boundary definition, object separation, and structural coherence?
answer: Paper A (SOAP) demonstrates via qualitative results on SemanticKITTI that its method produces distinct, separated car objects behind occluders and correctly discriminates fine-grained classes like road and sidewalk—whereas OccFormer fails on both counts, exhibiting fused cars and class confusion. Paper B (SGFormer) shows in Figure 4 that its 'Ours' reconstructions exhibit consistently clearer boundaries and more complete geometric structures compared to VoxFormer and Symphonies, especially in challenging regions such as intersections—highlighting superior structural coherence under complexity. Together, these figure-based observations illustrate how state-of-the-art methods are evaluated not just by metrics, but by interpretable visual hallmarks of semantic and geometric fidelity.

question: In papers on federated instruction-tuning of large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize both data quality properties and communication-efficiency versus task-performance trade-offs?
answer: In FedDQC, the Data Map visualization characterizes data quality by showing that low-quality data points—identified via ground truth—are clustered in the bottom-left corner (low confidence, low variance) and consistently receive low IRA scores on both pre-trained and fine-tuned models, confirming their persistent poor utility in federated instruction-tuning. In EcoLoRA, a comparative table quantifies the communication-efficiency versus task-performance trade-off: under 5 local updates, the FedIT baseline (a federated instruction-tuning method) achieves an ARC score of 66.3 with 1006.6 million upload parameters and 1971.3 million total parameters, whereas EcoLoRA achieves a comparable ARC score of 66.4 with drastically reduced upload cost (110.7 million) and total parameters (639.2 million), demonstrating improved efficiency without sacrificing instruction-tuning performance. The paper Optimizing Cross-Client Domain Coverage for Federated Instruction Tuning of Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that domain coverage — a data quality property reflecting cross-client domain diversity — correlates with task performance: for MMLU-Med, FedDCA achieves 74.50% accuracy with domain coverage 0.9348; for FPB, 72.93% with coverage 0.9815; and for GSM8K, 52.46% with coverage 0.9320.

question: In papers on Whole Slide Image Classification, how do figures or tables empirically quantify model performance under conditions that reflect real-world deployment challenges such as domain shift or method-specific enhancements?
answer: In 'GMMamba: Group Masking Mamba for Whole Slide Image Classification', Figure/Table evidence shows how the CSS scheme enhances WSI classification accuracy: ABMIL's accuracy improves from 0.827±0.092 to 0.866±0.086 (+3.9%) and TransMIL's from 0.796±0.101 to 0.822±0.135 (+2.6%) on the TCGA-ESCA dataset — demonstrating empirical gains from a method-specific enhancement. In 'HistoFS: Non-IID Histopathologic Whole Slide Image Classification via Federated Style Transfer with RoI-Preserving', Table 5 provides figure-based empirical evidence of robustness under domain shift: the HistoFS method with the Authenticity Module achieves balanced accuracy (bACC) of 82.50% and 85.53%, with F1-scores of 84.17% and 87.40%, on Unseen Institution D and E of the Camelyon17 dataset — directly quantifying performance on previously unseen clinical sites. The paper FOCUS: Knowledge-enhanced Adaptive Visual Compression for Few-shot Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that in Table 1, under the 4-shot setting for the TCGA-NSCLC dataset, the FOCUS (Ours) method achieves a Balanced ACC of 0.819±0.044, an AUC of 0.915±0.057, and an F1 Score of 0.819±0.067. The paper M3amba: Memory Mamba is All You Need for Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that in the ablation study on basic components (Table 4a), removing the Dynamic Memory Bank (DMB) results in a drop in Accuracy from 0.805 to 0.724, while removing the ConvBlock leads to a decrease in Accuracy from 0.805 to 0.609.

question: In papers on red teaming for text-to-image models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the properties of adversarial prompts generated by automated methods?
answer: Paper A (Automated Red Teaming for Text-to-Image Models...) uses Figure 4—a radar chart—to quantify the diversity of adversarial prompts across seven harm categories (Hate, Harassment, Violence, Self-Harm, Sexual, Shocking, Illegal activity), showing that FGPI with Seeds achieves higher scores than Naive and FGPI without Seeds across most categories. Paper B (AutoPrompt...) uses Figure 4—a multi-cell grid visualization—to qualitatively contrast prompt properties across four methods and four T2I models, demonstrating that its 'Ours' method consistently produces human-readable adversarial prompts without explicit blacklist words, whereas Ring-A-Bell, UnlearnDiffAtk, and P4D often include such words or yield semantically meaningless text.

question: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the relationship between vision-language architectural mechanisms and their impact on segmentation accuracy?
answer: Figure-based analysis in 'Effective SAM Combination for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation' details the Vision-Language Fusion (VLF) block as a core architectural mechanism: it applies sequential refinement to the correlation map using both vision attention (embedding and concatenating the correlation map with image features before transformer processing) and language attention (using text features as key/value to model inter-category relationships), directly shaping how visual and linguistic signals interact for segmentation. Meanwhile, table-based ablation results in 'Training-Free Class Purification for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation' empirically quantify the impact of architectural intervention—specifically FreeCP—on segmentation accuracy: it consistently improves mIoU across diverse backbones (ViT-L/14, OpenCLIP, R50x16), e.g., lifting mIoU from 46.0 to 58.9 on VOC21 with ViT-L/14, demonstrating that structural enhancements to class representation directly translate to measurable segmentation gains. The paper DPSeg: Dual-Prompt Cost Volume Learning for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that combining text and visual prompts (Avg(T,V)) improves mIoU across five open-vocabulary datasets (A-847, PC-459, A-150, PC-59, PAS-20) relative to using either modality alone — e.g., lifting scores from 10.4 to 12.0 on A-847 and from 93.4 to 96.0 on PAS-20 — demonstrating how architectural choices in prompt integration directly affect segmentation accuracy. The paper CLIPer: Hierarchically Improving Spatial Representation of CLIP for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that the segmentation results produced by CLIPer (Ours) are visually closer to the ground-truth images than those produced by MaskCLIP, SCLIP, ClearCLIP, and ProxyCLIP. The paper Images as Noisy Labels: Unleashing the Potential of the Diffusion Model for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that the DEDOS (Ours) model has 23.57 million learnable parameters, an inference time of 0.12 seconds, and 1030.47 GFLOPs, compared to CAT-Seg which has 70.27 million parameters, 0.37 seconds inference time, and 2000.57 GFLOPs.

question: In papers evaluating object hallucination mitigation in vision-language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses quantify performance using the CHAIR benchmark?
answer: Paper A (Look Twice Before You Answer) reports CHAIR evaluation results in Table 3 for the MemVR method, showing a CHAIR_S score of 46.6 (spatial hallucination rate), a CHAIR_I score of 13.0 (contextual hallucination rate), an Average score of 29.8, a Len score of 99.6, and a Recall score of 80.8. Paper B (Mitigating Object Hallucination...) presents CHAIR scores in Table 1 for multiple models and methods; specifically for LLaVA with MARINE, it reports 17.8 (Cs↓, spatial hallucination rate), 7.2 (Ct↓, contextual hallucination rate), and 50.8 (R↑, recall of ground-truth objects). Together, these table-based results demonstrate how CHAIR sub-metrics are empirically deployed to quantify distinct dimensions of hallucination reduction — with lower Cs↓/CHAIR_S and Ct↓/CHAIR_I indicating stronger suppression of spatial and contextual hallucinations, respectively, and higher R↑/Recall reflecting better alignment with visual content.

question: In papers on federated learning for large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the trade-off between communication cost and task performance across different fine-tuning methods?
answer: EcoLoRA reports that under 5 local updates, its w/ EcoLoRA method achieves an ARC score of 66.4 using 110.7 million upload parameters, while FedIT achieves a nearly identical ARC score of 66.3 but requires 1006.6 million upload parameters—demonstrating a tenfold reduction in upload cost for comparable performance. FedTT+ reports that its LLaMA2-13B (FedTT+) method achieves an average score of 87.70 with only 0.18M trainable parameters, compared to LoRA_r=8’s 6.55M parameters and 87.89 average score—highlighting a >36× reduction in parameter count for near-equivalent performance. Together, these figure-based results empirically characterize the steep diminishing returns in performance gain per unit of communicated parameters in federated LLM fine-tuning.

question: In papers on next POI recommendation, how do figure- or table-based analyses contextualize the Acc@1 metric across different evaluation conditions?
answer: The Geography-Aware LLM paper contextualizes Acc@1 through cross-city cold-start generalization: in figures/tables, it reports Acc@1 values for transfer scenarios such as training on NYC and testing on TKY (0.2594 for LLM4POI) or training on TKY and testing on CA (0.1960 for LLM4POI), highlighting model robustness across geographic domains. In contrast, the Refine-POI paper contextualizes Acc@1 through trajectory length stratification: its figures/tables break down Acc@1 by Short/Middle/Long trajectories, yielding values like 0.3341 (Short) and 0.3986 (Long) on NYC, and 0.2872 (Short) and 0.3357 (Long) on TKY—revealing performance sensitivity to sequence length rather than domain shift.

question: In papers on 3D human pose estimation, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize pose estimation accuracy using the Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) metric?
answer: Paper A reports MPJPE (and PA-MPJPE) in a figure/table for the 'downtown_bar' video, showing its method achieves MPJPE = 83.8 mm — reflecting performance under domain shift (e.g., synthetic-to-real adaptation). Paper B reports MPJPE in Figure 1 for four methods on a standard benchmark, with PoseAnchor achieving 40.3 mm — reflecting performance under controlled, likely in-distribution conditions. Both papers use MPJPE as a primary quantitative figure-based metric to empirically ground claims about pose estimation accuracy, though in distinct evaluation regimes: Paper A emphasizes robustness to domain shift in video, while Paper B emphasizes root-aware refinement on static or canonical test sets.

question: In papers on hallucination correction for multimodal large language models, how do figure- or table-supported case studies illustrate the nature of hallucinated content and its correction?
answer: Paper A ('Look Twice Before You Answer') uses Figure 9 to demonstrate correction of a numeric hallucination: for the question 'What is the price for tomatoes?', the default model and VCD generate incorrect numeric answers, while MemVR correctly outputs the ground-truth value 8.00 — illustrating precise quantitative hallucination mitigation in long-text generation. Paper B ('Nullu') presents two case studies (in its first figure/table context) showing correction of object-level semantic hallucinations: the original LLaVA model erroneously introduces 'person' and 'mountainous' when describing a painting of a dog, and 'pedestrians' when describing a highway scene; Nullu edits these outputs to remove the spurious entities, yielding accurate, hallucination-free descriptions focused solely on the depicted dog, highway, and traffic. The paper Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Image-Grounded Guidance provides figure-based evidence that MARINE corrects object hallucinations: for a query about a chair, LLaVA falsely asserts 'Yes, there is a white chair', while LLaVA w/ MARINE correctly responds 'No, there is no chair...'; and for captioning, LLaVA-v1.5 hallucinates 'toaster' whereas LLaVA-v1.5 w/ MARINE substitutes it with the grounded 'laptop'.

question: In papers on communication-efficient federated fine-tuning of language models, how do figure- or table-based empirical results characterize model performance on the ARC benchmark?
answer: Paper A (EcoLoRA) reports that both the FedIT and EcoLoRA methods achieve an ARC score of 66.4 under federated fine-tuning with 300 clients. Paper B (FedTT) reports that the FedTT method achieves an average score of 88.4 on the ARC benchmark using RoBERTa-Base — outperforming LoRA (88.3), BitFit (85.3), and Adapter (88.1) — demonstrating higher ARC performance under comparable efficiency constraints (0.06M trainable parameters). These figure-based results collectively show that different tensorized or low-rank adaptation strategies yield distinct ARC benchmark trade-offs in federated settings.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do figure- or table-based ablation studies characterize the impact of model components on detection performance, as measured by AVG mAP or AP?
answer: In 'CMHKF', an ablation study varying the CVKA parameter k (0–7) shows that component effectiveness peaks at k=2, yielding an AP of 86.57% and AVG mAP of 26.70%, with performance dropping at k=3 (AP=86.24%, AVG mAP=26.13%), indicating sensitivity to fusion granularity. In 'Learning Event Completeness', an ablation study of text enhancement strategies shows that combining vision-aware prompting (VAP) and prototype-based memory (PMB) yields the highest AVG mAP@IoU of 34.94 — notably higher than either alone (VAP-only: 32.73; PMB-only: 32.53) — demonstrating synergistic benefit from joint textual grounding mechanisms. Both papers use AVG mAP (or AP) in figures/tables to empirically ground architectural design choices, but differ in component type (parameterized fusion vs. modular text enhancement) and interaction pattern (univariate k-sweep vs. combinatorial module inclusion).

question: In domain-specific zero-shot composed image retrieval, how do figure-based analyses characterize the nature of common semantic failure cases?
answer: Figure-based analyses reveal two complementary categories of semantic failure: Paper A identifies failures rooted in abstract stylistic and relational attributes — for example, in the FashionIQ validation set, a query asking for 'the same design but light color and less flowy' incorrectly retrieves a floral-patterned shirt instead of one with a simpler design, indicating difficulty in aligning nuanced perceptual descriptors. Paper B identifies failures rooted in concrete compositional specifications — such as failing to replace 'woman' with 'man in a black suit and hat', omitting a 'golden frame' from a dog image cover, or inaccurately rendering 'brightly pastel blue walls and brown wooden flooring' in an indoor cafe setting — highlighting challenges in grounding precise object identities, structural elements, and scene-level attributes.

question: In papers on mathematical reasoning in large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the relationship between resource-constrained dimensions and model performance on standardized reasoning benchmarks?
answer: Paper A (GRPO-LEAD) uses a figure to show that GRPO+LEAD’s Pass@1 on AIME24 improves monotonically across increasing inference token budgets (2048–8192), outperforming baselines including DeepseekR1-7B (fixed Pass@1 = 0.409). Paper B (ClozeMath) uses a figure to show that DeepSeek-Math + ClozeMath’s GSM8K test accuracy rises from ~65% at 116 training steps to >74% at 928 steps, consistently exceeding the DeepSeek-Math + MFT baseline across all checkpoints. Together, these illustrate divergent figure-based strategies for linking resource allocation—either at inference time (token budget) or training time (optimization steps)—to gains in mathematical reasoning capability. The paper Safe: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via Retrospective Step-aware Formal Verification provides figure-based evidence that the Safe (Ours) method improves MATH accuracy over the LSTM (Ours) baseline by 1.5 points for GPT-4o and 4.2 points for Deepseek-Math, suggesting performance gains tied to step-aware formal verification — a resource-constrained dimension involving self-verification iterations. The paper Chain-of-Reasoning: Towards Unified Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via a Multi-Paradigm Perspective provides figure-based evidence that the multi-paradigm fine-tuning approach 'DSM + CoR (ours)' achieves 88.7 on GSM8k@1 and 66.7 on MATH@1 — the best scores in Table 5 — outperforming single-paradigm baselines.

question: In papers on multi-behavior learning for next POI recommendation, how do system architecture diagrams characterize the structural implementation of behavior-aware modeling?
answer: Paper A's system overview diagram explicitly defines a dedicated 'Multi-Behavior Learning' module that fine-tunes large language models using behavior-targeted prompts for predicting next POI, category, and region—reflecting a unified, prompt-driven, multi-output behavioral objective. In contrast, Paper B's architecture diagram decomposes behavior-awareness across three functionally distinct modules: the Graph-based User Preference Extractor processes categorical, distance, and temporal behavioral signals via Context-Adaptive Attention; the Sequential User Preference Extractor captures sequential behavior using a Transformer; and their interaction is formalized in the Graph-Sequential Mutual Enhancement Module via KL divergence alignment—indicating a modular, signal-disentangled, and alignment-based approach to integrating heterogeneous behavioral cues. The paper Refine-POI: Reinforcement Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that the Refine-POI framework architecture consists of a location-aware trajectory prompting module, a policy model (LLM), a reference model (LLM), and an update mechanism. The update mechanism calculates policy gradients using advantages derived from recommendation-driven rewards, which are composed of list format, reciprocal rank, soft accuracy, and distinction rewards. Dynamic sampling is applied to the responses before calculating advantages. The paper Efficient Model-Agnostic Continual Learning for Next POI Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that the GIRAM framework architecture, as shown in Figure 3, is divided into two stages: the Update Stage and the Deployment Stage—where behavior-aware modeling is implemented via context-aware key encoding, interest memory update, adaptive interest update, generative key-based retrieval, and adaptive interest fusion. The paper Geography-Aware Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that the GA-LLM framework implements behavior-aware modeling through a layered fine-tuning architecture: the GCIM module processes GPS-based spatial behavior using quadkey encoding and attention mechanisms (Q/K/V), while the PAM module aligns POI embeddings to capture semantic behavior via MLP-based alignment and tokenization.

question: In papers on medical vision-language models for chest X-ray interpretation, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize the impact of model modifications on clinical or task-specific performance?
answer: FactCheXcker demonstrates that updating models to incorporate measurement-aware supervision reduces median absolute error in endotracheal tube (ETT) placement estimation — e.g., GPT4V’s median error drops from ~4 cm to below 1 cm in violin plots comparing 'Original' vs. 'Updated' states — reflecting improved clinical grounding of spatial measurements. In contrast, Look & Mark reports table-based A.AVG scores showing consistent gains from incorporating radiologist eye fixations and bounding boxes: CXR-LLaVA improves from 73.21% to 74.40%, LLaVA-Med from 40.62% to 49.81%, LLaVA-OV from 47.14% to 65.69%, and Qwen2.5VL from 50.08% to 55.88%, illustrating enhanced holistic report generation accuracy through human-in-the-loop visual grounding. The paper Enhanced Contrastive Learning with Multi-view Longitudinal Data for Chest X-ray Report Generation provides figure-based evidence that MLRG(Ours) correctly reports 'the patient has received a right internal jugular vein catheter' for a relevant case, whereas the SEI-generated report omits this critical clinical detail and only states 'the course of the catheter is unremarkable'.

question: In papers on 3D Semantic Scene Completion, how do table-based evaluations characterize the overall and class-averaged semantic completion performance of leading methods?
answer: Paper A (Disentangling Instance and Scene Contexts) reports in Table 1 that its DISC method achieves an IoU of 45.32 and mIoU of 17.35 on the SemanticKITTI test set, with per-category breakdowns across 17 classes including road, building, car, vegetation, and person. Paper B (SGFormer) reports in Table 3 that its full satellite-ground fusion model achieves an IoU of 45.01 and mIoU of 16.68 on the same benchmark, alongside ablation evidence showing degradation when removing key components (Sat.-branch, Sat.-corr., Fusion), confirming the contribution of multi-source fusion to these scores. The paper SDFormer: Vision-based 3D Semantic Scene Completion via SAM-assisted Dual-channel Voxel Transformer provides figure-based evidence that its SDFomer method achieves an mIoU of 9.90 on the SemanticKITTI hidden test set, with per-class IoU scores including road (45.30), sidewalk (64.97), building (11.64), car (28.30), vegetation (7.31), person (11.49), pole (0.71), and traffic-sign (21.02). The paper SOAP: Vision-Centric 3D Semantic Scene Completion with Scene-Adaptive Decoder and Occluded Region-Aware View Projection provides figure-based evidence that its OAP method achieves an SC IoU of 47.24 and an SSC mIoU of 19.21, outperforming alternatives like simple Addition (SC IoU 45.00, SSC mIoU 18.05) and standard DCA (SC IoU 45.90, SSC mIoU 18.53).

question: In retrieval augmented generation systems that use knowledge graphs, how do figure- or table-based descriptions characterize the construction of graph-structured knowledge during offline indexing?
answer: E²GraphRAG constructs its knowledge graph through three indexing tasks: summarizing text chunks with an LLM to form a summary tree, extracting entities from each chunk using SpaCy, and merging subgraphs into a unified entity graph—yielding four data types (summary nodes, chunk nodes, entities, edges) and two mapping indexes (entity→chunks and chunks→entities). In contrast, HippoRAG 2 builds its knowledge graph via LLM-extracted triples, synonym detection using embeddings, and dense-sparse integration—producing a heterogeneous graph with Phrase Nodes, Passage Nodes, Seed Nodes, and three edge types (Relation, Synonym, Context Edges). These figure-based accounts highlight divergent design choices in node granularity, edge semantics, and index functionality within graph-based RAG indexing. The paper LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation provides figure-based evidence that its Graph-based Text Indexing stage constructs the knowledge graph through Entity & Rel Extraction, LLM Profiling, and Deduplication modules—offering an alternative indexing strategy where relational structure is first extracted, then semantically enriched via LLM profiling, and finally consolidated via deduplication.

question: In papers on mathematical reasoning in large language models, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance on the AIME benchmark?
answer: Paper A reports AIME performance as a function of synthesized data scale: AIME score improves from 27.0% to 33.0% as training data increases from +300k to +1.6M samples. Paper B reports AIME25 Pass@1 performance under varying inference budgets (2048–8192 tokens), showing GRPO+LEAD outperforms baselines including DeepseekR1-7B Best, which achieves a fixed Pass@1 of 0.283 (28.3%). Together, these figure-based results illustrate distinct empirical levers — data scale versus inference efficiency — that influence AIME-level reasoning capability.

question: In papers on Fake News Detection, how do table- or figure-reported quantitative evaluation metrics characterize model performance on benchmark datasets?
answer: The paper 'SARC: Sentiment-Augmented Deep Role Clustering for Fake News Detection' reports table-based evaluation results showing that the SARC model achieves a Macro-F1 score of 0.357 and RMSE of 0.761 on the RumourEval-19 dataset, and an Accuracy of 0.969, Precision of 0.967, Recall of 0.967, and F1-score of 0.967 on the Weibo-comp dataset — all best among compared methods. The paper 'FactGuard: Event-Centric and Commonsense-Guided Fake News Detection' presents in Table 2 an ablation result where removing the 'News' input feature from FACTGUARD leads to a macF1 score of 0.718 on the Weibo21 dataset, compared to the full model's score of 0.801 — demonstrating how table-based metrics quantify component-wise contributions to performance on a related Weibo-derived benchmark. The paper Disentangling Fact from Sentiment: A Dynamic Conflict-Consensus Framework for Multimodal Fake News Detection provides figure-based evidence that the hyperparameter sensitivity analysis reveals that for the Weibo dataset, the F1-real score peaks at a temperature coefficient (τ) of 1.5 and declines as the coefficient increases or decreases from this value. The paper ZoFia: Zero-Shot Fake News Detection with Entity-Guided Retrieval and Multi-LLM Interaction provides figure-based evidence that on the PolitiFact dataset, ZoFia (Ours) achieves an accuracy of 91.9 and an F1-score of 89.8, and on the GossipCop dataset, it achieves an accuracy of 78.5 and an F1-score of 61.2 — both highest among all listed methods for those datasets.

question: In papers on fake news detection, how do figure- or table-based analyses represent the structural or functional separation between fake and true news along semantic dimensions such as sentiment, factual consistency, or modality alignment?
answer: In 'SARC: Sentiment-Augmented Deep Role Clustering for Fake News Detection', t-SNE-based 3D projections on the Weibo-comp dataset visually demonstrate structural separation: fake news (n=48,570) and true news (n=53,656) form three distinct, compact clusters (green, yellow, blue) with clear inter-cluster boundaries—indicating that sentiment-augmented role features yield geometrically separable representations in embedding space. In 'Disentangling Fact from Sentiment: A Dynamic Conflict-Consensus Framework for Multimodal Fake News Detection', table-based calibration allocations on the GossipCop test set reveal functional separation: under Text Fabrication, the DCCF model assigns 68.2% confidence to Fact-Text (FT) versus 31.8% to Fact-Image (FI); under Image-Text Mismatch), it shifts to 20.7% for Sentiment-Text (ST) and 79.3% for Sentiment-Image (SI)—showing how the model dynamically partitions trust across fact- and sentiment-aligned modalities depending on the underlying deception mechanism.

question: In zero-shot composed image retrieval research on Fashion-IQ, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance using the ViT-G/14 backbone under the R@10 metric?
answer: The OSrCIR method achieves an average R@10 score of 37.57 on the Fashion-IQ validation set using ViT-G/14 (Reason-before-Retrieve paper). In contrast, the PrediCIR method reports a higher average R@10 of 47.2 on the same dataset and backbone (Missing Target-Relevant Information Prediction paper), with per-category scores of 39.7 (Dress), 48.2 (Shirt), and 53.7 (TopTee). Both results are derived from validation-set evaluations and reflect figure- or table-reported empirical performance under identical architectural and evaluation conditions.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do ablation studies in figures or tables quantify the impact of architectural components or training design choices on detection performance metrics?
answer: Paper A's ablation study quantifies how progressively adding modules and losses affects AUC on UCF-Crime: using only the PMG module with L_align yields 84.66 AUC; adding L_distill improves it to 85.84; and the full model with PMG, CMI, and all three losses (L_align, L_distill, L_PMG) achieves 90.33 AUC. Paper B's ablation study quantifies how varying the CVKA hyperparameter k affects AP and AVG mAP: k=2 yields the best performance (86.57% AP, 26.70% AVG mAP), while k=3 yields slightly lower results (86.24% AP, 26.13% AVG mAP). Together, these figure-based ablations empirically demonstrate how fine-grained design decisions — whether in loss composition, module integration, or cross-modality neighborhood size — are systematically evaluated via detection metrics in this task.

question: In papers on mathematical reasoning in large language models, what quantitative performance metrics do figure- or table-based evaluations report to assess model capability on standardized benchmarks?
answer: Paper A (GRPO-LEAD) reports Cons@32 (0.800 on AIME24, 0.567 on AIME25), Pass@1 (0.470 on AIME24, 0.345 on AIME25), and average token length (6,104 on AIME24, 6,308 on AIME25) — all derived from figure/table results on the AIME benchmarks. Paper B (Safe) reports accuracy scores (e.g., 79.6 for ORM1 ⊕ PRM1, 79.8 for ORM2 ⊕ PRM2, and 80.4 for Safe (Ours)) in an ablation analysis table evaluating GPT-4o on mathematical reasoning tasks using retrospective formal verification. Both papers use tabulated or plotted numerical outcomes to empirically ground claims about reasoning capability. The paper Chain-of-Reasoning: Towards Unified Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via a Multi-Paradigm Perspective provides figure-based evidence that Table 1 reports CoR-Math-7B achieving 66.0 on miniF2F-test and 66.7 on MATH — the highest scores among compared models on those benchmarks. The paper CogAtom: From Cognitive Atoms to Olympiad-level Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that CogAtom-long achieves scores of 91.2% on GSM8K, 83.0% on MATH500, 52.5% on AMC, 5/30 on AIME2024, and 3/30 on AIME2025 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-based models.

question: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation research, how do figure- or table-based evaluations demonstrate improvements in segmentation quality resulting from methodological advances?
answer: The DEDOS model (Images as Noisy Labels) demonstrates segmentation quality improvement quantitatively: on the MESS benchmark, its mean score rises from 35.9 with CLIP ViT-B/16 to 38.8 with CLIP ViT-L/14, indicating that stronger vision-language alignment enhances segmentation accuracy. Meanwhile, Training-Free Class Purification shows qualitative improvement visually: on COCO Stuff and ADE20K, baseline segmentations contain inaccuracies, but applying Redundancy Purification (+RP) removes incorrect classes, and further applying Ambiguity Purification (+AP Full) refines outputs to better match ground truth — a progression directly illustrated in figure visualizations. Together, these figure-based evaluations — one numeric, one visual — substantiate complementary pathways to improved segmentation fidelity. The paper DPSeg: Dual-Prompt Cost Volume Learning for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that in visualization examples, the proposed model outperforms SED [52] in segmenting small foreground objects like a mouse, bottle, and tennis racket — as shown in side-by-side comparisons with ground truth.

question: In papers on medical vision-language models for chest X-ray report generation, how do figures or tables empirically characterize the evaluated models in terms of their identities and diagnostic performance?
answer: FactCheXcker: Mitigating Measurement Hallucinations in Chest X-ray Report Generation Models presents a bar chart that quantitatively characterizes diagnostic performance by reporting pre- and post-intervention failure rates for ETT placement detection: GPT4V’s failure rate decreased from 90.0% to 12.5%, and LLM-CXR’s decreased from 75.3% to 15.5%. Look & Mark: Leveraging Radiologist Eye Fixations and Bounding boxes in Multimodal Large Language Models for Chest X-ray Report Generation provides a table or figure that empirically characterizes the evaluated models by listing six medical VLMs — CXR-LLaVA (8B, trained for Report Generation), MAIRA2 (7B, trained for Grounded Report Generation), LLaVA-Med (8B, trained for Medical Visual Question Answering), Llama3.2V (11B, trained for Image Understanding), LLaVA-OV (8B, trained for Visual Understanding), and Qwen2.5VL (8B, trained for Grounding and Visual Understanding) — thereby specifying model architectures, parameter scales, and task-aligned training objectives. The paper Enhanced Contrastive Learning with Multi-view Longitudinal Data for Chest X-ray Report Generation provides figure-based evidence that in the comparison on MIMIC-CXR, the MLRG(Ours) method achieves a B-4 score of 0.158 and an F1 score of 0.505, outperforming other methods like SEI [29] (B-4=0.135, F1=0.460) and Med-LLM [31] (B-4=0.128, F1=0.395).

question: In papers related to Biomedical Entity Linking, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance on the BC5CDR dataset in terms of precision-at-rank and recall-at-k behavior?
answer: The evaluation of model performance on the BC5CDR dataset is characterized through complementary figure- and table-based evidence: 'Guiding Large Language Models for Biomedical Entity Linking via Restrictive and Contrastive Decoding' reports precise Hits@1 scores in Table 5 — showing that LLM4BioEL achieves 88.4 (disease) and 96.0 (chemical) on BC5CDR, substantially improving over base Llama-3 models; meanwhile, 'BioEL: A Comprehensive Python Package for Biomedical Entity Linking' presents in Figure 4 recall@k curves (k = 1–10) demonstrating that BC5CDR consistently yields high recall, with all models exceeding 0.8 at k=10 — indicating strong top-k coverage despite variation in exact rank-1 accuracy. Together, these figure facts reveal that BC5CDR is a relatively high-performing benchmark where gains from advanced decoding (e.g., restrictive/contrastive) manifest strongly in exact match (Hits@1) and remain robust across the top-k ranking spectrum.

question: In camouflaged object detection research, how do figure- and table-based evaluations empirically characterize the segmentation accuracy and fidelity of proposed methods?
answer: Empirical characterization of segmentation accuracy and fidelity is provided through both quantitative metrics and representative visual comparisons. ESCNet reports quantitative results from ablation experiments on the NC4K dataset: its MFMM module—using all three branches (mask, edge, laplace)—achieves Fβ^w = 0.859, Eφ = 0.941, Sm = 0.892, and M = 0.028, indicating strong overall performance. Meanwhile, 'Enhancing Prompt Generation with Adaptive Refinement' provides qualitative visual evidence in Figure 5, where segmentation outputs of its method ('Ours') are shown to be consistently closer to ground truth than those of five competing methods (COMPrompter, ZoomNeXt, PRNet, FSNet, FSPNet) across four diverse sample images—demonstrating superior visual fidelity in challenging camouflage cases. The paper Improving SAM for Camouflaged Object Detection via Dual Stream Adapters provides figure-based evidence that the comparison of SAM-DSA and other methods on the COD task displays eight rows of test images, each showing the original input, ground truth, and predictions from SAM-COD, DSAM, MedSAM, SAM, ZoomNeXt, CamoFormer, FSPNet, and ZoomNet — visually demonstrating segmentation accuracy against ground truth across a different benchmark dataset. The paper UCOD-DPL: Unsupervised Camouflaged Object Detection via Dynamic Pseudo-label Learning provides figure-based evidence that the hyper-parameter ablation for the small-sized object ratio τ shows the model's performance is optimal and stable when τ is set around 0.15, as indicated by the peak and plateau of the metric curves in the chart.

question: In few-shot action recognition research, what empirical evaluation metrics are reported in tables to assess method performance?
answer: Papers report multiple table-based empirical metrics to evaluate few-shot action recognition methods. For example, TAMT reports resource-efficiency metrics in Table 3, including memory usage (1.9G), parameter count (2.8M), and training time (7.3 hours). D2ST-Adapter reports classification accuracy in Table 1, achieving 73.6% on the SSv2-Full dataset under the 5-way 5-shot setting — highlighted as the top result among compared methods. The paper Beyond Label Semantics: Language-Guided Action Anatomy for Few-shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that setting the number of atomic actions to 3 yields peak accuracy: 58.9% (1-shot) and 69.3% (5-shot) on HMDB51, and 86.8% (1-shot) and 89.3% (5-shot) on SSv2-Small. The paper Temporal Alignment-Free Video Matching for Few-shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that Table 5 lists FLOPs and parameter counts for various models, e.g., TEAM has 813 G FLOPs and 87.0 M parameters. The paper Trokens: Semantic-Aware Relational Trajectory Tokens for Few-Shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that Table 4 reports classification accuracy across multiple few-shot splits (e.g., 53.4% on SSV2 Small 1-shot, 76.7% on SSV2 Full 5-shot) and quantifies ablation impacts — e.g., disabling semantic-aware sampling reduces performance to 47.9% and 57.7% in those settings.

question: In papers on zero-shot composed image retrieval, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance on standard benchmarks using vision transformer backbones?
answer: PrediCIR reports mean Average Precision (mAP@k) on the COCO dataset using ViT-L/14 (mAP@5=15.7, mAP@10=17.1, mAP@25=18.6, mAP@50=19.3) and ViT-G/14 (mAP@5=23.7, mAP@10=24.6, mAP@25=25.4, mAP@50=26.0) backbones. CoTMR reports mAP@10=22.78 on the CIRCO benchmark and Recall@10=73.04 on the CIRR benchmark, both using a ViT-B/32 backbone. These results collectively demonstrate how different zero-shot CIR methods achieve varying levels of top-k retrieval accuracy across distinct benchmarks and backbone scales. The paper Reason-before-Retrieve: One-Stage Reflective Chain-of-Thoughts for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that ablation variants achieve CIRCO k=5 scores of 23.87 (full model removed) and 21.73 (one-stage reasoning removed). The paper Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Dual-Stream Instruction-Aware Distillation provides figure-based evidence that on the CIRCO test set, DistillCIR achieves an mAP@5 score of 16.31, an mAP@10 score of 16.90, an mAP@25 score of 18.54, and an mAP@50 score of 19.37; on the CIRR test set, it achieves R@1 of 29.88, R@5 of 58.75, R@10 of 70.26, R_s@1 of 62.33, R_s@2 of 82.46, and R_s@3 of 90.75. The paper Hierarchy-Aware Pseudo Word Learning with Text Adaptation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that the impact of the number of grouping modules (L) on performance shows that L=2 provides the highest average recall (R@1 + R@5) of 53.35. Performance decreases when L is set to 0, 1, 3, or 4.

question: In papers on federated instruction-tuning of large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses empirically characterize communication efficiency across different fine-tuning configurations?
answer: The paper 'Communication-Efficient and Tensorized Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models' reports that the FedTT+ method for LLaMA2-13B achieves an average score of 87.70 using only 0.18M trainable parameters, whereas the LoRA_r=8 baseline uses 6.55M parameters for a marginally higher score of 87.89 — demonstrating a parameter-count-based trade-off in communication efficiency. The paper 'EcoLoRA: Communication-Efficient Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models' provides time-based evidence: to reach a target accuracy of 66.5 on ARC, EcoLoRA's 'Full' configuration requires 18.2 minutes of upload time and 42.6 minutes of total time, while removing Round-Robin Segment increases upload time to 72.6 minutes and total time to 106.2 minutes — directly quantifying how architectural choices affect real-world communication overhead.
