The paper FedDQC: Data Quality Control in Federated Instruction-tuning of Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that FedDQC yields consistently higher inter-client model similarity on PubMedQA compared to FedAvg — indicating reduced model divergence and thus potentially lower communication overhead due to improved convergence stability under client heterogeneity.

question: In papers on few-shot action recognition, how do figure- or table-based empirical evaluations characterize model performance across different shot counts?
answer: Paper A reports in Table 1 that the TEAM model achieves 70.9% accuracy in the 1-shot setting and 85.5% in the 5-shot setting on HMDB51 using a ViT backbone. Paper B reports in Table 6 that its 'HoD (ours)' intra-motion module variant achieves 61.3% (1-shot) and 75.7% (5-shot) on SSV2 Full, while the 'Displacement only' ablation achieves 59.9% (1-shot) and 74.2% (5-shot) on the same dataset — collectively illustrating how different architectural choices yield distinct few-shot accuracy trends across shot counts, as empirically validated in tables. The paper Beyond Label Semantics: Language-Guided Action Anatomy for Few-shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that the CLUSTER method achieves 86.8% (1-shot) and 89.3% (5-shot) on HMDB51, while HARD achieves 87.3% (1-shot) and 89.3% (5-shot) on the same benchmark; on SSv2-Small, CLUSTER achieves 58.9% (1-shot) and 69.3% (5-shot), and HARD achieves 57.0% (1-shot) and 69.3% (5-shot). The paper TAMT: Temporal-Aware Model Tuning for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that Table 4(a) reports accuracy differences across datasets (SSV2: 59.18% vs. 40.45%; Diving: 45.18% vs. 28.09%; UCF: 95.92% vs. 94.69%) between TAA adapter + GTMT moment and no adapter + GAP moment — illustrating how architectural design choices affect empirical few-shot performance across multiple benchmarks.

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do figure- or table-based ablation studies characterize the functional role and necessity of modular components within their proposed editing architectures?
answer: LUSD uses an ablation study to quantify how individual design elements — such as 'Spatial Reg.', 'Normalize', 'Anneal (γ=1)', and 'Filtering' — contribute to CLIP-T (0.287 full vs. 0.265–0.279 ablated) and CLIP-AUC (0.074 full vs. 0.017–0.053 ablated) scores, showing that each module incrementally improves alignment with text guidance. SwiftEdit conducts a complementary ablation on its three-stage inversion framework — stage 1, stage 2, and IP-Adapter — demonstrating that omitting any one causes significant degradation across fidelity metrics: PSNR drops from 24.35 (full) to ≤22.11, LPIPS rises from 89.69 to ≥102.43, MSE increases from 4.59 to ≥6.28, and SSIM falls from 76.34 to ≤68.92. Together, these figure-based ablations reveal that both approaches rely critically on purpose-built, non-interchangeable modules — though differing in nature (regularization/annealing vs. staged inversion + adapter) — to achieve effective text-driven edits. The paper Training-Free Text-Guided Image Editing with Visual Autoregressive Model provides figure-based evidence that attention control — a modular component — improves handling of large modification areas and low-frequency changes, as demonstrated by the improved quality of edited images of a boy and a flower.

question: In papers on medical vision-language models for chest X-ray report generation, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the integration of anatomically precise visual grounding into model behavior or architecture?
answer: FactCheXcker demonstrates that anatomical precision is critical for clinical validity: a successful case study shows correction of an ET tube–carina distance from '6 cm' to the more accurate '4.24 cm', while failure cases reveal measurement errors of up to 5.0 cm when key landmarks (ET tube or carina) are mislocalized—highlighting how model hallucinations manifest as quantifiable spatial inaccuracies in generated reports. In contrast, Look & Mark proactively embeds anatomical grounding by augmenting the input with bounding boxes marking abnormal findings and radiologist eye fixation heatmaps converted into textual prompts—enabling the multimodal LLM to generate clinically relevant reports anchored to expert visual attention and spatial localization. Together, these figure-based insights illustrate two complementary approaches to achieving anatomical grounding: one through post-hoc measurement-aware fact verification, and the other through in-context visual cue injection during generation.

question: In studies of federated instruction-tuning of large language models, what benchmark-specific quantitative performance outcomes are reported for algorithmic approaches that address client-side data heterogeneity?
answer: FedDQC reports performance stability under decreasing data quality ratios: as the data quality ratio drops from 1.0 to 0.5, FedAvg shows significant performance degradation across PubMedQA, FiQA, AQUA-RAT, and Mol-Instructions, whereas FedDQC maintains relatively stable performance and consistently outperforms FedAvg on all four datasets. Separately, FedDCA reports benchmark-specific accuracy scores under four instruction-generation strategies: with Random Sampling, it achieves 71.80% on MMLU-Med, 63.92% on FPB, and 47.82% on GSM8K; with Direct Retrieval, 72.10% on MMLU-Med, 67.78% on FPB, and 52.53% on GSM8K; with LESS, 70.80% on MMLU-Med, 61.03% on FPB, and 43.92% on GSM8K; and with Self-Instruct, 70.70% on MMLU-Med, 60.21% on FPB, and 50.25% on GSM8K. Together, these figure-based results empirically characterize how distinct approaches—data quality control (FedDQC) and cross-client domain coverage optimization (FedDCA)—yield measurable, benchmark-anchored performance outcomes in response to client-side heterogeneity.

question: In papers on automated red teaming for text-to-image models, how do figure- or table-based analyses differ in characterizing the design of adversarial prompts versus the empirical evaluation of attack effectiveness?
answer: One paper presents a qualitative taxonomy of adversarial prompt strategies in Table 1, listing five categories—Visual Similarity, Cultural References, Unsafe Combination, Word Play, and Cultural Deficits—each accompanied by explanatory definitions, thereby characterizing *how attacks are conceptually designed*. In contrast, another paper uses a chart to show how Attack Success Rate (ASR) scales with reward model size for the FERRET (RM) method, reporting peak ASR values of 0.84 (Qwen-1.5-0.5B), 0.90 (Gemma-2B), 0.89 (phi-2), and 0.95 (Llama3-8B) against the Llama 2-chat 7B target model—thereby characterizing *how attack effectiveness is empirically evaluated and scaled*. Together, these figure-based analyses illustrate two complementary methodological axes: strategic categorization of prompt-level vulnerabilities versus quantitative calibration of scoring-based success. The paper AutoPrompt: Automated Red-Teaming of Text-to-Image Models via LLM-Driven Adversarial Prompts provides figure-based evidence that Table 3 quantifies how removing individual design components — unsafe image alignment, unsafe word alignment, perplexity constraint, and banned-token penalty — degrades the Red Teaming Success Rate (RSR), thereby characterizing *how adversarial prompt design choices are empirically grounded and causally validated*.

question: In papers on 3D semantic scene completion, how do figure-based qualitative results characterize the ability of methods to produce spatially coherent layouts and distinguish visually or contextually similar semantic classes?
answer: SOAP demonstrates distinct separation of occluded car instances behind other vehicles and correct differentiation between road and sidewalk—visual evidence indicating strong spatial reasoning and class boundary precision. DISC shows more logical scene layouts (e.g., roads not intersecting terrain) and more accurate, detailed instance predictions compared to Symphonies and CGFormer—visual evidence highlighting improved geometric consistency and instance-level semantic fidelity. Together, these figure-based findings illustrate complementary emphases: SOAP excels in occlusion-aware object separation and fine-grained class discrimination, while DISC emphasizes global layout plausibility and instance-aware detail recovery.

question: In papers on chest X-ray report generation, how do table-based ablation or intervention analyses characterize the impact of specific methodological choices on quantitative evaluation metrics?
answer: In 'FactCheXcker: Mitigating Measurement Hallucinations...', a performance comparison table shows that applying the FactCheXcker module improves factual grounding metrics: ETT Presence precision increases from 0.64 to 0.68 (CheXpertPlus), ETT Measurement MAE drops sharply from 2.35 to 0.39 (GPT4V), and ETT Placement precision rises from 0.74 to 0.97 (LLM-CXR), demonstrating gains in measurement and localization fidelity. In 'Enhanced Contrastive Learning with Multi-view Longitudinal Data...', an ablation table on the MIMIC-CXR test set shows that including clinical indications improves BLEU-2 from 0.253 to 0.295 and Rouge-L from 0.254 to 0.318, while including multi-view data improves BLEU-2 from 0.264 to 0.282 and Rouge-L from 0.266 to 0.301 — indicating that input conditioning via auxiliary clinical or imaging context enhances lexical and semantic fluency of generated reports. Together, these table-based analyses contrast two orthogonal improvement strategies: one enforcing factual consistency via post-hoc verification, the other enriching input representation for better language generation. The paper Look & Mark: Leveraging Radiologist Eye Fixations and Bounding boxes in Multimodal Large Language Models for Chest X-ray Report Generation provides figure-based evidence that the average number of clinically significant errors per generated report varies across model variants: 1.75 for CXR-LLaVA (L&M), 1.75 for MAIRA2 (-), 1.88 for LLaVA-OV (I&L&M), 2.12 for Qwen2.5VL (I&L&M), and 2.18 for CXR-LLaVA (-).

question: In papers on few-shot action recognition evaluated on the SSv2-Full benchmark, how do figure- or table-based results characterize model performance under the 5-shot setting?
answer: Trokens reports a 5-shot action recognition accuracy of 76.7% on SSv2-Full, while D2ST-Adapter’s dual-branch configuration 'aDSTA-S & aDSTA-T' achieves 73.6% on the same dataset and setting. Both values are derived from controlled experimental evaluations presented in tabular form, directly quantifying comparative model capability under the standardized 5-shot protocol on SSv2-Full. The paper TAMT: Temporal-Aware Model Tuning for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that SSL pre-training followed by TAMT tuning achieves a 5-shot action recognition accuracy of 59.18% on the SSv2-Full benchmark.

question: In papers on federated fine-tuning of large language models, how do figure- or table-based results characterize the empirical performance trade-offs between communication efficiency and model effectiveness?
answer: Figure-based results in EcoLoRA show that communication time dominates total execution time across all tested network conditions (UL/DL 0.2/1 Mbps to 5/25 Mbps), with total time decreasing from ~2000s to ~120s as bandwidth increases — demonstrating its communication-efficiency profile. In contrast, figure-based results in the Communication-Efficient and Tensorized Federated Fine-Tuning paper show that FedTT+ achieves test accuracy rising from ~65% to >90% on QNLI within 10 communication rounds in a 50-client cross-silo setting — demonstrating strong task effectiveness under limited rounds. Together, these figure facts empirically ground complementary dimensions of performance: EcoLoRA’s figures emphasize time and bandwidth sensitivity (efficiency), while the second paper’s figures highlight rapid accuracy gain per round (effectiveness), jointly illustrating how different methods navigate the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off in federated LLM fine-tuning.

question: In papers related to retrieval-augmented question answering, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance on the MuSiQue benchmark?
answer: The MuSiQue benchmark is used to empirically evaluate different aspects of RAG systems: 'From RAG to Memory' reports passage-level retrieval effectiveness via recall@5 scores on the MuSiQue dev set (e.g., 80.5 at reset weight 0.05), reflecting how well the method retrieves supporting passages; in contrast, 'LP-RAG' reports answer-generation quality via exact-match (EM = 32.6) and F1 (69.1) scores on MuSiQue, capturing end-to-end multi-hop reasoning fidelity. Together, these figure-based metrics illustrate complementary empirical lenses — retrieval coverage versus answer correctness — applied to the same benchmark. The paper LINEARRAG: LINEAR GRAPH RETRIEVAL AUG-MENTED GENERATION ON LARGE-SCALE CORPORA provides figure-based evidence that, on MuSiQue, Vanilla RAG (Top-5) achieves Evidence Recall of 71.85%, Context Relevance of 62.87%, and Accuracy of 61.68%, while HippoRAG achieves 74.57%, 42.64%, and 55.04%, respectively — offering a decomposition-aware, multi-faceted evaluation of retrieval, relevance filtering, and answer accuracy.

question: In papers addressing object hallucination mitigation in vision-language models, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance on the POPE benchmark?
answer: The paper 'Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Image-Grounded Guidance' reports in Table 2 that MARINE achieves POPE scores of 66.9 (Accuracy↑), 72.9 (F1↑), and 72.3 (Yes%) for LLaVA. The paper 'Look Twice Before You Answer: Memory-Space Visual Retracing for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models' reports in Table 4 that MemVR achieves an average POPE accuracy of 86.93 and an average F1-score of 85.59 across Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings. Together, these table-based results empirically characterize how distinct architectural strategies—image-grounded guidance versus memory-space visual retracing—quantify improvements on the POPE benchmark. The paper Nullu: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via HalluSpace Projection provides figure-based evidence that Nullu achieves POPE Accuracy of 79.52±0.04, Precision of 93.46±0.03, and F score of 91.79±0.04 for LLaVA-1.5; Accuracy of 71.92±0.39, Precision of 95.96±0.65, and F score of 92.07±0.65 for MiniGPT-4; and Accuracy of 77.09±1.37, Precision of 92.83±0.29, and F score of 90.80±0.52 for mPLUG-Owl2.

question: In papers evaluating 3D human pose estimation on the Human3.6M dataset, how do figure- or table-based analyses differ in their use of MPJPE to support method evaluation?
answer: In PoseAnchor, MPJPE is presented in Table 1 as a consolidated, action-averaged performance metric — specifically, the average MPJPE is reported as 40.3 on Human3.6M, alongside P-MPJPE (32.1), Abs-MPJPE (103.3), and MRPE (96.7), reflecting end-to-end pose estimation accuracy under standard evaluation. In contrast, HiPART uses MPJPE not as a final score but as a diagnostic signal: Figure/Table 4 shows how MPJPE performance changes with codebook dimension on Human3.6M, revealing diminishing returns beyond 128 and peak performance at 2048 (sparse tokens) and 3072 (dense tokens), thereby treating MPJPE as a trend-sensitive indicator of architectural capacity effects rather than a static benchmark value.

question: In papers on adversarial evaluation of text-to-image models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the influence of model configuration or target model identity on adversarial prompt effectiveness?
answer: Paper A uses Figure 5(a) to show that attack success rate increases with guidance scale (e.g., from 88.57% to 92.86% at image size 1024 when guidance scale rises from 2.5 to 12.5), while simultaneously maintaining high safety (Figure 5(b): 98.57% safe prompts at size 1024, guidance scale 2.5), indicating that adversarial effectiveness is sensitive to inference-time configuration within a given model. In contrast, Paper B’s Table 4 demonstrates that adversarial prompt effectiveness varies dramatically across target models — e.g., P4D-N prompts achieve 100% success on ESD but only 9.76% on AdvUnlearn — revealing that target model identity (and its underlying safety mechanisms) critically determines transfer-based adversarial success.

question: In papers on mobile task automation, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize the accuracy performance of vision-language models for grounding natural language instructions to GUI elements?
answer: The R-VLM paper reports quantitative grounding accuracy results on two benchmarks: on ScreenSpot, R-VLM achieves 75.1 average grounding accuracy (vs. 73.3 for UGround); on Multimodal-Mind2Web, it achieves 48.9 average element accuracy (vs. 46.3 for UGround). The UI-E2I-Synth paper reports accuracy for two model variants on UI-I2E-Bench: UI-I2E-VLM-7B achieves 69.5 average accuracy (72.0 on Explicit instructions, 67.9 on Implicit), while UI-I2E-VLM-4B achieves 53.4 average accuracy (61.9 on Explicit, 48.3 on Implicit). Together, these figure-based evaluations demonstrate how model scale, instruction type (explicit vs. implicit), and benchmark design influence measured GUI grounding accuracy in mobile task automation systems. The paper DiMo-GUI: Advancing Test-time Scaling in GUI Grounding via Modality-Aware Visual Reasoning provides figure-based evidence that grounding accuracy (%) increases from 18.4 at 0 iterative zooming steps to a peak of 48.9 at 5 steps, after which it plateaus.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the integration of textual information as a modality?
answer: Paper A's framework architecture explicitly integrates textual information via a 'Cross-modal Anomaly-aware Branch' that uses a CLIP Text Encoder to process anomaly category descriptions, followed by a Prototype-based Attention Block and Self-Attention to fuse text prototypes with video features before MIL classification. Paper B's evaluation table shows that modality combinations including text—specifically Video+Text (AP = 84.81%, AVG mAP = 24.32%) and Video+Audio+Text (AP = 86.57%, AVG mAP = 26.70%)—achieve the top two performance scores among four tested multi-modality configurations, empirically affirming the functional value of text as a complementary modality under weak supervision.

question: In papers on federated instruction-tuning of large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses jointly characterize the trade-off between communication efficiency, model uniformity across clients, and instruction-following capability?
answer: EcoLoRA demonstrates that parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA rank 32) can maintain strong instruction-following capability—achieving an ARC score of 66.8—while drastically reducing upload parameters (333.5M vs. 2600.4M) and total parameters (2567.5M vs. 5117.0M) compared to baseline FFA-LoRA, indicating a favorable communication-efficiency–performance trade-off. FedDQC complements this by showing improved model uniformity: its similarity matrix on PubMedQA exhibits consistently higher inter-client similarity across all pairs—including Client 5—compared to FedAvg’s lower and more variable similarity values, suggesting that data-quality-aware aggregation reduces model divergence without explicit parameter compression. Together, these figure-based findings reveal two orthogonal yet synergistic pathways—structured parameter update compression (EcoLoRA) and data-aware client-level alignment (FedDQC)—to jointly improve communication efficiency, model uniformity, and instruction-following capability in federated LLM tuning. The paper Communication-Efficient and Tensorized Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that the FedTT algorithm workflow involves clients sending only updated tensor factors — rather than full adapter parameters — to the server for aggregation, enabling communication-efficient updates while preserving structured model uniformity through shared tensorized representations. The paper Optimizing Cross-Client Domain Coverage for Federated Instruction Tuning of Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that domain coverage — a measure of cross-client domain alignment — varies with ξ: for Med, coverage ranges from 0.9348 (ξ=10) to 0.9618 (ξ=80); for Fin, it remains stable near 0.9815; and for Math, it peaks at 0.9348 (ξ=20), suggesting domain-dependent sensitivity to aggregation scope and offering a complementary figure-based perspective on model uniformity under data heterogeneity.

question: In papers on federated instruction tuning, how do figure- or table-based empirical evaluations characterize model performance—through absolute task scores or relative improvements over federated optimization baselines?
answer: Paper A ('Optimizing Cross-Client Domain Coverage...') characterizes performance using absolute task scores: when paired with FedDCA, different instruction selection strategies yield concrete accuracies—e.g., 72.10% on MMLU-Med with Direct Retrieval, 52.53% on GSM8K, and 67.78% on FPB. In contrast, Paper B ('FedDQC: Data Quality Control...') characterizes performance via relative improvements over federated optimizer baselines on PubMedQA: +7% over FedAvg, +5.3% over FedAvgM, +2.2% over FedAdagrad, +1.4% over FedYOGI, and +5.5% over FedAdam—demonstrating how data quality control quantitatively lifts baseline performance rather than reporting standalone scores. The paper Communication-Efficient and Tensorized Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that under severe data heterogeneity, the RoBERTa-Large (FedTT+) method achieves an average score of 89.40, while RoBERTa-Large (LoRA_r=2) achieves 77.93—characterizing performance via absolute task scores.

question: In papers related to mathematical reasoning, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model capability across different difficulty regimes and model families?
answer: The CogAtom paper characterizes capability through absolute performance on high-difficulty, proof- and reasoning-intensive benchmarks: its figure/table reports 90.8% accuracy on math500 (a curated test of advanced problem-solving), and concrete counts of correct solutions on real AIME exams (10/30 on AIME2024 and 9/30 on AIME2025), highlighting ceiling performance at the Olympiad level. In contrast, the ClozeMath paper characterizes capability through relative improvement trends across model scales on the arithmetic-word-problem benchmark GSM8K: its figure/table shows consistent gains over MFT baselines — +77.10 accuracy for DeepSeek-Math, +75.97 for Llama-3.1-8B, +57.39 for Llama-3.2-3B, and +31.84 for Llama-3.2-1B — emphasizing scalability and transfer robustness rather than absolute ceiling. The paper Chain-of-Reasoning: Towards Unified Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via a Multi-Paradigm Perspective provides figure-based evidence that the PPT strategy’s cumulative performance improves across stages on both MATH (47.9 → 61.0 → 66.7) and GSM8K (61.0 → 73.6 → 88.7), bridging Olympiad-level and arithmetic-word-problem regimes within a single ablation framework. The paper GRPO-LEAD: A Difficulty-Aware Reinforcement Learning Approach for Concise Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models provides figure-based evidence that on the AIME24 benchmark, the LEAD-stage2 model achieves a Cons@32 score of 0.867, a Pass@1 score of 0.650, and an average token length of 8,267. On the AIME25 benchmark, it achieves a Cons@32 score of 0.767, a Pass@1 score of 0.539, and an average token length of 8,668. The paper Safe: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models via Retrospective Step-aware Formal Verification provides figure-based evidence that on the MATH dataset, the Safe (Ours) method achieves 80.4 accuracy with GPT-4o and 52.4 with Deepseek-Math, while the LSTM (Ours) baseline achieves 78.9 and 48.2 respectively — demonstrating relative improvement across model families on a difficulty-graded benchmark.

question: In papers related to GUI grounding, how do figure- or table-based evaluations quantify model performance across platforms or functional subcategories?
answer: R-VLM (R-VLM: Region-Aware Vision Language Model for Precise GUI Grounding) reports grounding accuracy on the GroundUI-1K dataset segmented by platform: 76.5% on Web, 65.3% on Desktop, and 79.7% on Mobile, yielding an average of 74.1%. WinSpot (WinSpot: GUI Grounding Benchmark with Multimodal Large Language Models) evaluates models on its benchmark with subcategory breakdowns: Uground achieves 27.2% on File Management, 51.4% on System Settings, 45.4% on Productivity Tools, and 82.4% on MS Store & Web, resulting in an overall accuracy of 44.2%; in contrast, general-purpose multimodal models like GPT-4o and GPT-4V achieve only 16.5% and 18.3% overall, respectively. These figure-based metrics illustrate divergent evaluation granularities—platform-centric vs. task-subcategory-centric—and highlight the importance of benchmark-specific reporting conventions in GUI grounding assessment. The paper DiMo-GUI: Advancing Test-time Scaling in GUI Grounding via Modality-Aware Visual Reasoning provides figure-based evidence that the +DiMo-GUI variant achieves higher grounding performance than its Vanilla counterpart across six functional subcategories—CAD, Creative, Dev, Office, OS, and Sci—as visualized in the radar chart of Figure 2. The paper UI-E2I-Synth: Advancing GUI Grounding with Large-Scale Instruction Synthesis provides figure-based evidence that the UI-E2I-Synth-Web model achieves higher accuracy than OS-Atlas-Web across all platform–subcategory combinations on ScreenSpot: e.g., 89.0 vs 35.2 on Mobile Text, 93.3 vs 67.0 on Desktop Text, and 79.6 vs 70.9 on Web Text.

question: In papers on Whole Slide Image Classification, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the improvement of class discriminability in learned feature representations?
answer: GMMamba characterizes discriminability improvement through its Cross-group Super-feature Sampling (CSS) module: it constructs a final super-feature representation f_sgr by combining cross-attention outputs (f_s^ca) and multi-head attention refinements (f_s^mha) using an Association Matrix Q derived from Max-Pooled group features (f_s^max), thereby explicitly modeling inter-group dependencies to enhance representational expressiveness. Flow-MIL characterizes discriminability improvement via t-SNE visualization and kernel density estimation (KDE): the 2D t-SNE plot shows markedly better separation between positive and negative instances in the Latent Semantic Embedding Space (LSES) after invertible flow transformation, and the KDE overlap area between classes decreases from 0.729 in the original complex feature space to 0.568 in LSES—providing quantitative evidence of enhanced class separability. The paper FOCUS: Knowledge-enhanced Adaptive Visual Compression for Few-shot Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that the variant including all modules (BaseMIL, Prompt, KAVTC, SVTC, CrossAgg) achieves a Balanced ACC of 0.864±0.032 on the UBC-OCEAN dataset under the 16-shot setting — the highest value reported in Table 2 for that setting.

question: In lidar-based methods for 3D semantic scene completion, how do figure- or table-based ablation studies characterize the contribution of individual architectural components to overall performance, as measured by IoU and mIoU?
answer: SDFormer's ablation study quantifies component contributions on the SemanticKITTI validation set: using only the Geometric Refiner achieves 43.85 IoU and 15.43 mIoU; adding the Semantic Constructor improves these to 44.89 IoU and 16.12 mIoU; and incorporating both with LMG and SSI yields 45.10 IoU and 16.01 mIoU. SGFormer's ablation study reports that the full model—including Satellite branch, Satellite correlation, and Fusion components—achieves 45.01 IoU and 16.68 mIoU, with degradation observed when any one component is disabled, confirming each contributes positively to performance. Together, these figure-based ablations demonstrate how modular architectural design is empirically validated via metric-wise decomposition in lidar-based scene completion. The paper Disentangling Instance and Scene Contexts for 3D Semantic Scene Completion provides figure-based evidence that Table 5 shows ablation of the Adaptive Instance Layer, where combining Instance Self-Attention, Instance-Image Cross-Attention, and Instance-Scene Cross-Attention yields 17.05 mIoU.

question: In papers evaluating zero-shot composed image retrieval on Fashion-IQ, how do qualitative figure-based results characterize the extent to which different models visually realize specified textual attribute manipulations?
answer: Paper A's qualitative result shows that for the query 'is black t-shirt with Star Wars image print', the proposed model retrieves both a correct black t-shirt with Star Wars print and an incorrect blue t-shirt with a similar print—indicating partial success in preserving the graphic while failing on color constraint; in contrast, Context-I2W retrieves a black t-shirt with a different graphic and a white t-shirt, revealing failures in both graphic and color fidelity. Paper B's qualitative result shows that for a query modifying dress color and sleeve length, the HIT model successfully retrieves images matching the modified description (e.g., correct color + adjusted sleeve length), whereas Pic2Word retrieves visually similar dresses that ignore the textual modifications—demonstrating HIT’s stronger alignment with compositional text instructions and Pic2Word’s reliance on visual similarity over attribute-level editing. Together, these figure-based observations contrast how different architectures prioritize and execute multi-attribute textual edits in Fashion-IQ retrieval.

question: In papers on camouflaged object detection, how do figure- or diagram-based architectural descriptions characterize the structural organization of feature processing and cross-modal interaction?
answer: ESCNet structures feature processing through a collaborative, multi-module architecture: its network comprises an Encoder, an Adaptive Edge-Texture Perceptor (AETP), multiple Dual-Stream Feature Augmentors (DSFA), and multiple Multi-Feature Modulation Modules (MFMM), indicating a design focused on parallel edge-semantics integration and iterative feature refinement within a single forward pass. In contrast, 'Improving SAM for Camouflaged Object Detection via Dual Stream Adapters' adopts a sequential, bidirectional knowledge distillation pipeline: first distilling knowledge from a pre-trained image encoder to a fine-tuned RGB adapter, then performing modal distillation from that RGB adapter to a fine-tuned depth adapter — reflecting a staged, modality-aware transfer strategy rather than integrated feature augmentation. These two figure-based architectural depictions illustrate divergent design philosophies — one emphasizing intra-network collaborative modules, the other prioritizing staged cross-modal knowledge alignment.

question: In papers on 3D human pose estimation, how do table- or ablation-based evaluations quantify pose estimation error in relation to design choices affecting input representation or root localization?
answer: Paper A's Table 6 evaluates root position estimation using robust least squares regression methods, reporting that the ZS-anchor method achieves the lowest Abs-MPJPE (107.7 mm) and MRPE (100.5 mm) among five compared approaches — directly linking regression strategy to root localization accuracy. Paper B's ablation study quantifies the impact of hierarchical 2D pose input resolution on overall pose accuracy: using a 96-joint input yields an MPJPE of 42.7 mm, while expanding to a 192-joint input only marginally improves MPJPE to 41.4 mm despite nearly doubling model parameters (2.5M → 4.4M), illustrating the diminishing returns of higher-granularity input representations on end-to-end pose error. The paper Semantics-aware Test-time Adaptation for 3D Human Pose Estimation provides figure-based evidence that adding Alignment improves MPJPE from 87.7 to 79.3 and PA-MPJPE from 53.8 to 49.6; adding 2D EMA further improves MPJPE to 78.0 and PA-MPJPE to 48.7; and adding 2D Fill-in achieves the best results with MPJPE of 76.4 and PA-MPJPE of 47.2.

question: In papers on Grammatical Error Correction evaluation, what figure- or table-based analyses characterize the empirical behavior of evaluation components under parameter variation?
answer: The paper 'Rethinking Evaluation Metrics for Grammatical Error Correction' uses window analysis (N=8) to show that integrating TrueSkill consistently improves the Pearson correlation coefficient of the IMPARA metric with human judgment across all starting ranks (1–7), as visualized by the solid blue line remaining above the dashed blue line in the figure. Meanwhile, 'Targeted Syntactic Evaluation for Grammatical Error Correction' reports in a figure that CTSEG's edit coverage declines from ~70% to ~35% as the BEA-train frequency threshold increases from 1 to 16, and remains consistently higher than CoNLL-2014 and BEA-dev across all thresholds — demonstrating how dataset coverage responds empirically to filtering parameters.

question: In papers on whole slide image classification, how do table-based evaluations quantify model performance across benchmark datasets and experimental conditions?
answer: Paper A (HistoFS) reports table-based performance metrics on the Camelyon17 dataset: for unseen institutions D and E, the HistoFS method with the Authenticity Module achieves balanced accuracy (bACC) of 82.50% and 85.53%, and F1-scores of 84.17% and 87.40%, respectively. Paper B (Flow-MIL) provides table-based ablation results on the CAMELYON16 dataset: removing reconstruction loss (w/o L_rec), latent alignment loss (w/o L_latent), or LSP guidance yields instance-level AUCs of 0.9246, 0.9231, and 0.9189, and corresponding bag-level AUCs of 0.9378, 0.9025, and 0.8987 (ablation study table). Together, these illustrate how table-based evaluations capture diverse aspects of WSI classifier performance — including cross-institution generalization and component-wise contribution analysis under controlled ablations. The paper M3amba: Memory Mamba is All You Need for Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that the M3amba model's performance on the TCGA BRCA dataset is 0.931±0.024 for Accuracy, 0.971±0.005 for AUC, 0.956±0.035 for Precision, and 0.957±0.022 for Recall, which are the highest values among all listed methods in Table 1. The paper FOCUS: Knowledge-enhanced Adaptive Visual Compression for Few-shot Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that on the UBC-OCEAN dataset under 16-shot settings, the CONCH model achieves the highest Balanced ACC (~0.86), followed by GPFM (~0.84), Virchow (~0.83), PLIP (~0.82), and UNI (~0.81). The paper GMMamba: Group Masking Mamba for Whole Slide Image Classification provides figure-based evidence that the complete GMMamba model achieves an accuracy of 0.949±0.029, AUC of 0.970±0.033, and F1 of 0.955±0.025 on the TCGA-ESCA dataset, and removing the CSS component reduces accuracy to 0.924±0.055.

question: In papers on camouflaged object detection, how do figure- and table-based evaluations jointly characterize the effectiveness of newly proposed methods?
answer: The visual evaluation in Figure 5 of 'Enhancing Prompt Generation with Adaptive Refinement for Camouflaged Object Detection' demonstrates that the proposed method ('Ours') produces segmentation masks visually closer to ground truth than five baselines (COMPrompter, ZoomNeXt, PRNet, FSNet, FSPNet) across four diverse sample images — providing qualitative evidence of superior perceptual fidelity. Complementing this, Table 1 in 'Improving SAM for Camouflaged Object Detection via Dual Stream Adapters' quantitatively validates effectiveness across four standard COD datasets (CAMO, CHAMELEON, COD10K, NC4K), showing that SAM-DSA achieves top-ranked scores (highlighted in red/blue/orange) across multiple metrics (M, F^w, S_m, E^x, alphaE), and is explicitly identified as a SAM-based method (dagger symbol); notably, CHAMELEON — the dataset named after the shared keyword — is included as a core benchmark. Together, these figure-based evidences establish a dual-axis validation: visual plausibility on representative cases and statistical dominance across standardized benchmarks including the chameleon-specific dataset. The paper UCOD-DPL: Unsupervised Camouflaged Object Detection via Dynamic Pseudo-label Learning provides figure-based evidence that for the pseudo-label mixing strategy ablation on the COD10K dataset, the APM strategy yields the best results across all metrics compared to Proportional(1:1) Mixing and Linear Decay Mixing, with values of .834 for S_m, .763 for F_β^ω, .779 for F_β^m, .916 for E_φ^m, and .031 for M.

question: In GUI grounding research, how do benchmark datasets and associated evaluations empirically characterize the scope of supported applications and the effectiveness of grounding models on interactive task execution?
answer: Empirical grounding evidence is provided across two major benchmarks: WinSpot characterizes scope through its domain-wise application coverage — specifically, File Management (16.3%), System Settings (7.1%), Productivity Tools (12.2%), and MS Store & Web (9.2%) — with concrete examples including Windows Explorer, Task Manager, Microsoft Word, Outlook, Teams, Settings App, Terminal, and Edge/Chrome (WinSpot paper). AutoGUI, in contrast, characterizes effectiveness via task-level performance: on the AITW benchmark, its integration yields an Avg Step accuracy of 39.23% using Gemini-2.0-flash-exp as planner and Qwen2-VL-7B SFT fine-tuned with AutoGUI as grounding model — representing a +9.73 absolute improvement over the baseline (AutoGUI paper). Together, these figure- and table-supported facts jointly define GUI grounding evaluation along two essential dimensions: real-world application coverage and interactive task execution capability. The paper DiMo-GUI: Advancing Test-time Scaling in GUI Grounding via Modality-Aware Visual Reasoning provides figure-based evidence that for the OS-Atlas-7B model integrated with DiMo-GUI, the grounding performance scores are 96.2 for Mobile Text, 73.5 for Mobile Icon/Widget, 96.4 for Desktop Text, 75.1 for Desktop Icon/Widget, 89.7 for Web Text, and 75.4 for Web Icon/Widget, resulting in an overall average of 85.7. The paper R-VLM: Region-Aware Vision Language Model for Precise GUI Grounding provides figure-based evidence that the IoU distribution for R-VLM predictions on the GroundUI-1K benchmark is shifted towards higher IoU values compared to the baseline, as shown by the histograms for both Web and Desktop environments, indicating more precise localization. The paper UI-E2I-Synth: Advancing GUI Grounding with Large-Scale Instruction Synthesis provides figure-based evidence that on the OSWorld benchmark, the +UI-I2E-VLM setting achieves an overall success rate of 12.0, compared to 8.5 for +OS-Atlas and 3.6 for Screenshot only*.

question: In papers proposing graph-structured or link-aware retrieval-augmented generation frameworks, how do figure- or table-based empirical evaluations characterize indexing time as a system performance metric?
answer: LP-RAG reports indexing times ranging from 4.7 to 7.9 minutes across five multi-hop QA datasets (HotpotQA-S, MuSiQue-S, MultiHop-S, RAG-QA-S, ICLR-S), reflecting its link prediction–based indexing overhead. LINEARRAG reports two indexing times: 2745.94 seconds (~45.8 minutes) for its G-retriever baseline and 249.78 seconds (~4.2 minutes) for its optimized LinearRAG method — demonstrating how architectural design (e.g., linearized graph traversal) significantly reduces indexing latency. Together, these figure-based measurements empirically ground indexing time as a critical, quantifiable trade-off between graph expressivity and preprocessing efficiency in structured RAG systems. The paper E^2GraphRAG: Streamlining Graph-based RAG for High Efficiency and Effectiveness provides figure-based evidence that for the NovelQA dataset with the Qwen model, the indexing time for E²GraphRAG is approximately 1400 seconds for a 700k token document, which is significantly lower than GraphRAG (approx. 50,000s) and LightRAG (approx. 30,000s), and comparable to RAPTOR (approx. 10,000s).

question: In papers on Grammatical Error Correction, what quantitative evaluation metrics are reported in figures or tables to assess either model performance or dataset coverage properties?
answer: The paper 'Enhancing Text Editing for Grammatical Error Correction: Arabic as a Case Study' reports macro average F0.5 scores — a model-level performance metric — for two GEC models (4-Ensemble: 71.9; SWEET: 71.6) on the QALB-2014 Dev set. The paper 'Targeted Syntactic Evaluation for Grammatical Error Correction' reports edit coverage — a dataset-level metric — for the CTSEG evaluation suite, showing its coverage decreases from ~70% to ~35% as the frequency threshold for BEA-train increases from 1 to 16, while remaining consistently higher than coverage for CoNLL-2014 and BEA-dev across all thresholds. The paper Reliability Crisis of Reference-free Metrics for Grammatical Error Correction provides figure-based evidence that Table 2 reports quantitative model-level metrics — including SOME_G(·), SOME_F(·), SOME_M(·), ppl(·), LDR(·), TSR(·), QE(·), and SE(·) — for adversarial outputs of GEC systems SUCH AS SOME, Scribendi, and IMPARA. The paper Rethinking Evaluation Metrics for Grammatical Error Correction: Why Use a Different Evaluation Process than Human? provides figure-based evidence that for the IMPARA metric on the SEEDA-E dataset with the +Fluency configuration, the Pearson correlation coefficient using TrueSkill (w/ TrueSkill) is 0.981, and the Spearman correlation coefficient is 0.982, representing the highest values in their respective columns for that configuration.

question: In zero-shot composed image retrieval research using ViT-G/14 backbones, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize the role of retrieval accuracy metrics—such as R@1 or R@10—in assessing method performance across different benchmarks and method families?
answer: The 'Generative Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval' paper uses Table 4 to show that LinCIR + CIG-XL turbo with ViT-G/14 achieves the highest average R@1 score (13.48) among LinCIR variants on the GeneCIS test set, highlighting top-1 precision as a key metric for compositional generalization in that setting. In contrast, the 'Reason-before-Retrieve' paper reports in its results that OSrCIR with ViT-G/14 attains an average R@10 score of 37.57 on the Fashion-IQ validation set—outperforming CIREVL* (32.62) and differing from LinCIR (45.11)—indicating that top-10 recall is emphasized to capture broader compositional alignment in fashion-oriented retrieval. Together, these table-based findings illustrate how R@1 and R@10 serve complementary roles in evaluating ViT-G/14-based models depending on benchmark semantics and method architecture. The paper Hierarchy-Aware Pseudo Word Learning with Text Adaptation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that for the CIRR test set, the HIT method achieves R@1 scores of 27.9 (CLIP) and 36.9 (BLIP), and R@50 scores of 90.4 (CLIP) and 94.7 (BLIP); and for the Fashion-IQ validation set, it achieves an Average R@10 score of 34.5 and an Average R@50 score of 55.8. The paper CoTMR: Chain-of-Thought Multi-Scale Reasoning for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval provides figure-based evidence that Recall@K performance on Fashion-IQ and CIRR varies systematically with hyperparameters λ and μ — increasing then stabilizing or declining with λ, and peaking then decreasing with μ — illustrating how retrieval accuracy metrics respond to architectural tuning in ViT-G/14-based zero-shot composed image retrieval. The paper Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Dual-Stream Instruction-Aware Distillation provides figure-based evidence that DistillCIR with ViT-G/14 achieves R@10 scores of 30.73 (Shirt), 25.51 (Dress), and 33.88 (Toptee) and R@50 scores of 50.12 (Shirt), 46.64 (Dress), and 53.74 (Toptee) on the FashionIQ validation set.

question: In papers on large language models for next point-of-interest recommendation, how do figure- or table-based ablation studies characterize the impact of removing key model components or learning mechanisms on Acc@1 performance?
answer: The Geography-Aware LLM paper reports Acc@1 degradation in cross-city cold-start scenarios: for example, when trained on NYC and tested on TKY, removing the POI-Aware Memory (PAM) module increases Acc@1 from 0.2594 (LLM4POI) to 0.3018 (w/o PAM); similarly, when trained on TKY and tested on CA, removal of PAM raises Acc@1 from 0.1960 to 0.2273—suggesting PAM introduces a context-specific trade-off. In contrast, the Refine-POI paper’s ablation on NYC shows that removing the reward component reduces Acc@1 from 0.3469 (full model) to 0.2300, while removing location information reduces it to 0.3180—indicating both reward shaping and location grounding contribute positively to top-1 accuracy, with reward having a larger marginal effect. Together, these figure-based findings quantify how distinct architectural and learning-level components influence Acc@1 under different experimental configurations.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do figure-based architectural diagrams characterize the functional role and integration mechanism of textual prompts relative to visual inputs?
answer: CMHKF treats textual prompts as a co-equal third input stream—encoded by a CLIP Text Encoder and processed through an FFN module—then fused symmetrically with audio and video streams via CVKA and MKAF modules before binary classification. In contrast, LEC-VAD uses textual descriptions solely to instantiate category priors; these are encoded by a CLIP Text Encoder and processed by a Prototype-based Attention Block, which then modulates video features (from CLIP Image Encoder + Local Transformer + Global GCN) via Self-Attention before feeding into a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) module—reflecting an asymmetric, guidance-oriented role for text rather than symmetric fusion.

question: In research on target element localization in GUIs, how do figure- or table-based characterizations of benchmark design — such as element density, annotation granularity, and instruction implicitness — relate to empirical distributions of localization accuracy?
answer: The relationship is illustrated by synthesizing evidence from R-VLM and UI-E2I-Synth: R-VLM's histogram shows the SeeClick baseline achieves predominantly low IoU scores (<0.5) across Web, Desktop, and Mobile environments on the ScreenSpot benchmark, indicating systematic localization difficulty. UI-E2I-Synth's comparative table reveals ScreenSpot has a higher landscape element-to-screen ratio (0.088 vs. 0.042), lacks fine-grained type annotation and implicitness annotation, and exhibits lower minimum type proportion (3.21% vs. 12.34%) compared to UI-I2E-Bench — suggesting that sparser, coarser, and less semantically nuanced benchmark design may correlate with poorer observed localization accuracy. Thus, benchmark structural and annotation properties provide contextual grounding for interpreting empirical accuracy distributions. The paper AutoGUI: Scaling GUI Grounding with Automatic Functionality Annotations from LLMs provides figure-based evidence that the AutoGUI dataset exhibits high annotation richness (17.9M tokens in Train split, avg. 23.1 words/annotation) and broad domain coverage (916 unique apps), with balanced device distribution in Test (50% Web / 50% Mobile).

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do figure- or table-based algorithmic descriptions characterize the mechanism for controlling editing strength and region-specific fidelity?
answer: Paper A describes a 'Randomness caching' algorithm (Algorithm 1) that controls editing behavior through iterative scale-wise computation of probability distributions and attention maps, which are cached as bit labels and pushed into queues — enabling fine-grained stochastic control over latent token generation without training. Paper B introduces the Attention Rescaling for Mask-aware Editing (ARaM) process, where editing strength is controlled via a normalized editing mask M derived from source and edit noise maps, and further tuned using two global scaling parameters: s_x balances edit semantic fidelity against background preservation, and s_y governs the intensity of modification within the masked region — both explicitly parameterized and visualized in the algorithmic flow. The paper LOCATEdit: Graph Laplacian Optimized Cross Attention for Localized Text-Guided Image Editing provides figure-based evidence that the text-guided image editing pipeline includes a Selective Embedding Interpolation module and a Dual Branch Denoising Paradigm featuring a CASA Graph for optimization — enabling region-specific fidelity control through graph Laplacian-regularized cross-attention. The paper LUSD: Localized Update Score Distillation for Text-Guided Image Editing provides figure-based evidence that the method controls editing strength and region-specific fidelity through a 'Mask (Mk)' generated from intermediate diffusion model activations, which guides 'Gradient Filtering and Normalization' to produce an 'Update Gradient' applied iteratively to the current image.

question: In papers on next POI recommendation, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model behavior on the CA dataset?
answer: Figure-based evaluations on the CA dataset provide complementary empirical insights: in 'Geography-Aware Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation', an ablation study shows that removing the GCIM component causes the largest drop in Acc@1 (from 0.2566 to 0.2402), indicating its critical role in accuracy; removing Fourier or PAM components yields smaller drops (to 0.2467 and 0.2499, respectively). In 'Efficient Model-Agnostic Continual Learning for Next POI Recommendation', Figure 5 presents memory usage (in MB) across methods and backbones on CA — e.g., with Flashback backbone, ReLoop2 consumes ~18,000 MB while GIRAM uses only ~6,000 MB — revealing substantial variation in computational footprint. Together, these figure-supported facts empirically characterize both predictive performance and system-level efficiency of next POI recommendation models on the CA dataset.

question: In papers on chest X-ray report generation, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the incorporation of auxiliary information beyond raw images?
answer: One paper evaluates auxiliary information through ablation-based quantitative performance: the 'Images + effective sources (h=0)' model — which integrates non-image patient-derived data — achieves superior scores across multiple metrics (RG: 30.4, CX: 35.7, CB: 79.1, G: 41.6, BS: 37.5, R-L: 32.2, B4: 8.7, ARN: 93.5) compared to benchmarks like CXRMate-RRG24. Another paper characterizes auxiliary information through a structured visual grounding workflow: the Look & Mark framework incorporates radiologist-derived bounding boxes ('Mark') and eye fixation heatmaps converted to text ('Look') to construct in-context prompts for multimodal LLMs, enabling clinically grounded report generation. The paper FactCheXcker: Mitigating Measurement Hallucinations in Chest X-ray Report Generation Models provides figure-based evidence that the FactCheXcker pipeline architecture consists of three sequential modules — a Query Generator, a Code Generator using domain-specific tool modules (e.g., T1 for Endotracheal Tube Detection), and a Report Updater — enabling auxiliary information integration via tool-augmented code generation. The paper Enhanced Contrastive Learning with Multi-view Longitudinal Data for Chest X-ray Report Generation provides figure-based evidence that on the MIMIC-CXR dataset, removing auxiliary inputs — such as clinical indications (F1 drops from 0.505 to 0.479), multi-view data (F1 drops to 0.476), or multi-view longitudinal data (F1 drops to 0.498) — degrades report generation performance, demonstrating their distinct contributions through ablation.

question: In papers on hallucination mitigation for multimodal large language models, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the operational implementation and empirical evaluation of visual grounding strategies?
answer: Paper A characterizes visual grounding through an architectural diagram and description showing that the Memory-space Visual Retracing (MemVR) method re-injects visual tokens into the middle trigger layer of the text decoder via a Feed Forward Network (FFN), contrasting it with logits-level modification in Visual Contrastive Decoding (VCD). Paper B characterizes visual grounding through Figure 3—a set of three line charts demonstrating how varying guidance strength (γ) affects CHAIRs (decreasing from ~0.25 to 0.15) and Recall (increasing from 0.40 to 0.50) across LLaVA, LLaVA-v1.5, and mPLUG-Owl2—thereby empirically linking parameterized image-grounded guidance to quantitative hallucination reduction. The paper Nullu: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via HalluSpace Projection provides figure-based evidence that for the word 'people', the frequency under Nullu (90) is lower than under LLaVA (115) but higher than under VCD (66). The paper Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models with Assembly of Global and Local Attention provides figure-based evidence that the Image-Prompt Matching module architecture includes an input image, a matching model computing similarity sim(v,t), an adaptive masking component, and a GradCAM visualization yielding a masked image where irrelevant regions are removed based on the correlation score. The paper ICT: Image-Object Cross-Level Trusted Intervention for Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models provides figure-based evidence that the t-SNE visualization for layer 16 shows Image-Level vectors (blue and yellow) are relatively close, indicating similarity in encoding image-level information, while Object-Level vectors (red and green) are more distinct; in layer 18, both Image-Level and Object-Level vectors exhibit high similarity between LLaVA-v1.5 and Qwen-VL models.

question: In papers on next POI recommendation, how do figure- and table-based analyses characterize the output behavior of recommendation models?
answer: The Geography-Aware Large Language Models paper uses tabular results (Figure/Result in Section 4.3) to quantify output behavior by reporting the proportion of successful predictions where the target POI is absent from the input sequence — specifically, 2.85% (LLM4POI) and 4.36% (w/o GCIM) on CA, and 1.5% (LLM4POI) and 2.5% (w/o GCIM) on NYC — revealing how models handle unseen targets. The Efficient Model-Agnostic Continual Learning paper provides a map-based visualization (Figure 16) showing the top-5 recommended POI locations as orange dots for User #137 across five temporal blocks (T2–T5), illustrating the spatiotemporal evolution and geographic distribution of model outputs over time. Together, these figure-based analyses empirically ground output behavior in both quantitative success rates under target-absence conditions and qualitative spatial-temporal structure of recommendations. The paper Knowledge Graph Tokenization for Behavior-Aware Generative Next POI Recommendation provides figure-based evidence that circles representing POIs from the same category form noticeable clusters in the StruID visualization on the FB dataset — indicating category-coherent spatial organization in model outputs.

question: In papers on text-guided image editing, how do qualitative result grids characterize the visual behavior and editing fidelity of proposed methods?
answer: Paper A (LUSD) presents a qualitative results grid comparing edits across seven prompts (e.g., '+ dog', '(British → Canadian) flag', '+ hot air balloon'), where its method ('Ours') consistently preserves the background while successfully adding or replacing the specified object — demonstrating strong structural localization and context retention. Paper B (SwiftEdit) shows a comparative visual chart across diverse edits (e.g., 'two birds' → 'two origami birds', 'yellow bird' → 'crochet bird'), where its method ('Ours') achieves high-fidelity semantic transformations with minimal artifacts and is annotated with a runtime of < 0.3s — highlighting simultaneous semantic precision, visual cleanliness, and computational efficiency. Together, these figure-based analyses reveal complementary facets of editing fidelity: Paper A foregrounds spatial integrity and compositional stability, while Paper B foregrounds conceptual controllability and real-time viability. The paper Training-Free Text-Guided Image Editing with Visual Autoregressive Model provides figure-based evidence that the decoded results during the generation process show that as the scale k increases, the image evolves from containing only low-frequency information (overall structure) to higher-frequency details, which can be preserved during editing.

question: In fake news detection studies using the GossipCop dataset, how do figure- or table-based ablation analyses characterize the relative impact of different model components on classification performance?
answer: Paper A's Table 2 shows that ablating the 'w/o News' component reduces F1_real from 0.935 to 0.924 and F1_fake from 0.675 to 0.623, indicating a larger degradation on fake-class detection. Paper B's ablation study reports overall F1-score reductions on GossipCop: removing Open Web retrieval drops F1 from 61.2 to 58.1 (−3.1), Wikipedia retrieval to 59.9 (−1.3), both external sources to 58.2 (−3.0), linguist analysis to 58.9 (−2.3), expert analysis to 57.3 (−3.9), both analyses to 58.9 (−2.3), claim verification to 60.5 (−0.7), and the debate component to 59.2 (−2.0). Together, these figure-based results quantify how distinct architectural choices — news-aware modeling versus multi-source retrieval and multi-role analysis  — yield different sensitivity patterns to component removal, with expert analysis (−3.9) and 'w/o News' (−0.051 drop in F1_fake) showing comparatively high impact in their respective designs.

question: In papers on open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, how do figure-based architectural descriptions characterize the approach to enhancing spatial representation within CLIP-based frameworks?
answer: DPSeg enhances spatial representation through a Cost Volume-Guided Decoder (CVGD) that integrates multi-scale visual features (D1, D2, D3) with unified embeddings (E, V, T) derived from a CLIP Image Encoder, Visual Prompt Encoder, and CLIP Text Encoder — enabling structured cost-volume reasoning over pixel-level correspondences. In contrast, CLIPer adopts a hierarchical strategy: an early-layer fusion module processes raw patch embeddings from the CLIP image encoder to generate a coarse segmentation map, which is then refined by a fine-grained compensation module that explicitly incorporates attention maps from Stable Diffusion to recover high-frequency spatial details. The paper Images as Noisy Labels: Unleashing the Potential of the Diffusion Model for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation provides figure-based evidence that the proposed framework's architecture enhances spatial representation through three coordinated parts: (a) Proxy Queries for Scene Skeleton — comprising an Encoder, Noise Predictor, Decoder, and Interaction Module; (b) Separation of Texture Information — using a CLIP Image Encoder to process denoised images; and (c) Feature Refinement and Cross-modal Interaction — integrating a CLIP Text Encoder and Transformer Decoder for prediction.

question: In papers on few-shot action recognition, how do figure- or table-based empirical evaluations characterize model performance in terms of accuracy across shot levels and inference efficiency?
answer: Trokens (Paper A) reports few-shot accuracy on FineGym in Table 5: Trokens achieves 84.4% (1-shot), 88.3% (3-shot), and 89.9% (5-shot), outperforming TATs and MoLo at all shot levels. Beyond Label Semantics (Paper B) presents a bar chart comparing methods on HMDB51, where the proposed method achieves 86.8% accuracy and an inference time of 187.82ms—higher accuracy than CLIP-FSAR (80.9%) and faster than Qwen-2.5† (5.80s), though slightly slower than CLIP-FSAR (189.54ms). Together, these figure-based results empirically characterize both accuracy scaling with shot count and trade-offs between accuracy and inference speed in few-shot action recognition. The paper TAMT: Temporal-Aware Model Tuning for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that TAMT achieves 77.82% accuracy on HMDB and 97.08% on UCF101 in Table 1, expanding the empirical accuracy characterization across multiple few-shot action recognition benchmarks. The paper Temporal Alignment-Free Video Matching for Few-shot Action Recognition provides figure-based evidence that Figure 7 compares computational time for video matching, showing that for a number of frames greater than 32, the computational time for TEAM increases linearly, whereas for OTAM and TRX, it increases quadratically.

question: In papers related to demonstration selection for in-context learning, how do figure- or table-based analyses and algorithmic procedures jointly characterize the relationship between demonstration selection strategy and model performance?
answer: The relationship is characterized as one where raw demonstration count (k) alone is insufficient to maximize performance, and explicit selection strategy critically modulates outcomes. In 'Sample Efficient Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning', Table 2 shows non-monotonic performance trends across k-shot settings: on GSM, accuracy peaks at 5-shot (73.46) and drops at 7-shot (68.84); similarly on StrategyQA, it peaks at 5-shot (73.06) and declines at 7-shot (70.61) — indicating diminishing or negative returns from adding more demonstrations without strategic curation. Complementing this, 'Linear-Time Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning via Gradient Estimation' introduces Algorithm 2 (ICL-GRADRE), which implements a selection strategy grounded in gradient-based scoring: it samples random subsets, estimates per-example scores using ICL-GRADEx, computes average scores, and selects the k demonstrations with the *lowest* scores — formalizing a principled, computationally efficient mechanism to operationalize selection in light of such performance saturation. Together, these figure- and algorithm-based evidences establish that effective demonstration selection must balance quantity with quality-aware ranking, rather than relying on uniform k-shot enumeration. The paper Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning via Reinforcement Learning provides figure-based evidence that on BANKING77, reinforcement learning–based selection methods RDES/B (0.718) and RDES/C (0.843) substantially outperform zero-shot (0.394) and AdaEmbedding (0.689) baselines — illustrating how distinct selection strategies yield markedly different performance outcomes.

question: In papers proposing graph-based RAG methods, how do figure- or table-based analyses characterize the retrieval mechanism and its empirical effectiveness?
answer: E²GraphRAG characterizes its retrieval mechanism through a process diagram that specifies a multi-stage pipeline: it begins with entity extraction from the query; when entities are present, it applies Graph Filtering to retain core entity pairs, followed by Index Mapping to identify candidate chunks, and finally Entity-aware Ranking to select top-k chunks — with local retrieval operations highlighted in light yellow and global ones in light green. LightRAG, in contrast, provides empirical evaluation evidence in Table 1, reporting win rates (%) against four baselines (including GraphRAG) across four datasets (Agriculture, CS, Legal, Mix) and four evaluation dimensions (Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Empowerment, Overall); for example, on the Agriculture dataset, LightRAG achieves a 67.6% win rate over NaiveRAG specifically on Comprehensiveness. Together, these figure-based accounts jointly inform how graph-based RAG retrieval is both architecturally designed and quantitatively validated. The paper LINEARRAG: LINEAR GRAPH RETRIEVAL AUG-MENTED GENERATION ON LARGE-SCALE CORPORA provides figure-based evidence that in Table 1, for the Medical dataset, the LinearRAG method achieves a GPT-Accuracy of 63.72%, which is the highest value in that column. The paper LP-RAG: A LINK PREDICTION-BASED FRAMEWORK FOR RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION provides figure-based evidence that in the Q&A results on five datasets, LP-RAG achieves the highest accuracy and F1 scores across all benchmarks: 89.32 Acc and 86.29 F1 on HotpotQA-S, 89.67 Acc and 85.15 F1 on MuSiQue-S, 89.12 Acc and 86.35 F1 on MultiHop-S, 87.89 Acc and 85.26 F1 on RAG-QA-S, and 91.16 Acc and 89.51 F1 on ICLR-S. The paper From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models provides figure-based evidence that HippoRAG 2’s retrieval mechanism produces filtered knowledge triples (e.g., '(I. P. Paul, from, Thrissur)') and expands final results beyond the top entity (e.g., returning 'Thrissur' and 'Yinka Ayefele' for 'In what city was I.P. Paul born?'), thereby illustrating both its graph-aware filtering logic and empirical retrieval behavior on Simple and Multi-Hop QA tasks.

question: In papers on few-shot action recognition, how do table-based empirical analyses characterize the sensitivity of model accuracy to configurable structural parameters that govern task or representation granularity?
answer: Trokens uses Table 3 to show how N-way 1-shot classification accuracy degrades monotonically as the number of classes increases—from 61.5% at 5-way to 49.1% at 10-way on SSV2 Full, and from 82.9% to 73.3% on Kinetics—demonstrating task complexity sensitivity. In contrast, Beyond Label Semantics uses its analysis to show that accuracy peaks at exactly 3 atomic actions on HMDB51 (58.9% 1-shot, 69.3% 5-shot) and SSv2-Small (86.8% 1-shot, 89.3% 5-shot), with lower performance at 1, 2, or 4 atomic actions—revealing an optimal granularity threshold for action decomposition. Together, these table-supported findings illustrate divergent yet complementary strategies: one treating granularity as a fixed task constraint (N-way), the other as a tunable representational hyperparameter (atomic action count).

question: In papers on few-shot action recognition, how do figure- or table-based evaluations characterize model performance in terms of few-shot accuracy across standard video action datasets?
answer: Paper A (Trokens) reports in-domain few-shot accuracy on SSV2 Full and Kinetics: on SSV2 Full, it achieves 61.5% (1-shot) to 76.7% (5-shot); on Kinetics, it achieves 82.9% (1-shot) to 91.2% (5-shot) — demonstrating strong scaling with shot count in a standard few-shot setting. Paper B (TAMT) reports cross-domain few-shot accuracy after temporal-aware tuning: on SSV2 (target), it achieves 59.18%; on Diving, 45.18%; and on UCF, 95.92% — all under a fixed few-shot protocol (implied by the paper’s focus and evaluation design), showing that domain-adaptive tuning significantly improves few-shot transfer over baseline fine-tuning (e.g., +10.19% on SSV2, +11.59% on Diving, +6.19% on UCF). question: In papers addressing object hallucination mitigation in vision-language models, how do figure-based architectural descriptions characterize the integration of visual grounding signals during the LLM decoding process?

question: In next POI recommendation, how do different methodological approaches—such as generative knowledge-aware modeling versus model-agnostic continual learning—differ in their dependence on the choice of underlying prediction backbone or baseline architecture?
answer: The generative knowledge-graph tokenization method KGTB demonstrates robust superiority over all conventional (non-generative) baselines—including graph-based methods—suggesting its performance is not contingent on matching a specific backbone family and instead derives stability from its knowledge-grounded generation process. In contrast, the model-agnostic continual learning method ReLoop2 shows strong performance when paired with Flashback but suffers notable degradation with GETNext and DiffPOI, indicating its error memory and targeted replay mechanism is highly sensitive to backbone-specific characteristics such as temporal modeling capacity or denoising structure. This contrast reveals a trade-off: architectural generativity can confer cross-paradigm robustness, whereas modular continual adaptation may require careful backbone alignment. The paper Refine-POI: Reinforcement Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation points out that Graph-based models such as STP-UDGAT, HMT-GRN, DRGN, GETNEXT, and STHGCN address the cold-start issue by leveraging graph structures to capture spatio-temporal relationships, collaborative signals, or higher-order interactions, but they fail to integrate contextual information with commonsense knowledge.

question: In zero-shot composed image retrieval, how do different architectural strategies balance instruction-following capability with computational efficiency during training and inference?
answer: DistillCIR (Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Dual-Stream Instruction-Aware Distillation) addresses this balance by using a dual-stream distillation framework that transfers instruction-following capability from large language models (LLMs) to lightweight projection-based models; it achieves superior performance over existing LLM-based ZS-CIR models while remaining efficient in model size and requiring no LLMs during inference. In contrast, PrediCIR (Missing Target-Relevant Information Prediction with World Model for Accurate Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval) employs a predictor-based world model to recover missing target-relevant information, yielding significant performance gains (1.73–4.45% across six ZS-CIR tasks) but at higher training cost (28 hours — 6 hours longer than Pic2Word and 18 hours longer than SEARLE) and larger model size due to its prediction-based mapping; however, it maintains fast inference (0.03s), only marginally slower than LinCIR and four times faster than diffusion-based CompoDiff (0.12s). The paper CoTMR: Chain-of-Thought Multi-Scale Reasoning for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval points out that Existing methods for ZS-CIR primarily combine caption models and Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate target captions from composed queries but face issues such as incompatibility, visual information loss, and insufficient reasoning. The paper Reason-before-Retrieve: One-Stage Reflective Chain-of-Thoughts for Training-Free Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval points out that the proposed model uses a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) Ψ_M to generate a target image description T_t from a reference image I_r and a manipulation text T_m, using a Reflective Chain-of-Thought prompt p_c; the description is then used for CLIP-based retrieval via cosine similarity, enabling training-free instruction-following with modular reasoning. The paper Hierarchy-Aware Pseudo Word Learning with Text Adaptation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval points out that previous pseudo-word methods ignore the hierarchical nature of editing objects and lack text adaptation capability, thus failing to adapt to multi-level editing needs.

question: In multi-instance learning frameworks for whole slide image classification, how do different methods design the aggregation of sparse and spatially dispersed instance features into discriminative bag-level representations?
answer: GMMamba addresses this by introducing an intra-group masking Mamba (IMM) module that performs location-based grouping and feature selection within Mamba’s state-space architecture, followed by a cross-group super-feature sampling (CSS) module that explicitly aggregates sparse and dispersed tumor features across groups to improve bag representation. In contrast, FOCUS employs a three-stage progressive and adaptive visual compression strategy: it first removes global redundancy via coarse-grained filtering, then leverages pathology foundation models and domain-specific prompts to guide semantic relevance–based visual token compression, and finally applies neighbor-aware fine-grained filtering and cross-modal aggregation to generate the slide-level representation—all within a knowledge-enhanced multi-instance learning framework tailored for few-shot WSI analysis. The paper Flow-MIL: Constructing Highly-expressive Latent Feature Space For Whole Slide Image Classification Using Normalizing Flow points out that extensive experiments on three public WSI datasets show that Flow-MIL outperforms recent SOTA methods in both bag-level and instance-level classification and offers improved interpretability. The paper M3amba: Memory Mamba is All You Need for Whole Slide Image Classification points out that the M3amba method employs a BiMamba Block for inter-group instance fusion and intra-group representation learning, and develops a novel dynamic memory bank (DMB) to retain long-range information, achieving efficient yet effective performance.

question: In automated chest X-ray report generation, how do hallucinations manifest across different linguistic and clinical dimensions of the generated text, and what implications do these patterns have for clinical reliability?
answer: Hallucinations in chest X-ray report generation manifest both broadly in semantic content and specifically in quantitative measurements—two dimensions with distinct clinical implications. Paper A identifies that language models used to generate reports from patient data are prone to bias and hallucination, potentially producing clinically incorrect content due to overreliance on auxiliary inputs without sufficient imaging grounding. Paper B demonstrates that medical vision-language models frequently hallucinate quantitative measurements (e.g., lesion size, cardiac silhouette dimensions, pleural effusion volume), which directly undermines clinical reliability because such values inform diagnosis, staging, and treatment decisions. Together, these findings indicate that hallucinations are not merely generic 'factual errors' but occur along a spectrum—from high-level diagnostic misattributions to precise numerical inaccuracies—necessitating dimension-aware evaluation and mitigation.

question: In biomedical entity linking, how do different methodological approaches differ in their treatment of ontology integration, model flexibility, and inference mechanism?
answer: Methodological approaches to biomedical entity linking vary significantly along these dimensions. BENT (BioEL: A Comprehensive Python Package for Biomedical Entity Linking) implements a fixed graph-based approach tightly integrated with 14 pre-specified ontologies and domain-specific pre-processing dictionaries; it performs end-to-end named entity recognition and linking but explicitly restricts users to this single methodology and does not support alternative models or linking techniques. In contrast, most contemporary BioEL methods fall into two broad classes: discriminative methods—which encode mentions and candidate entities using BERT-based models and retrieve top candidates via embedding similarity (often followed by cross-encoder reranking)—and generative methods—which directly produce linked entity identifiers or names using task-specific language modeling. This highlights a fundamental contrast: BENT prioritizes structured, ontology-grounded reasoning within a rigid pipeline, whereas mainstream discriminative and generative approaches emphasize model flexibility, learned semantic matching, and decoupled or end-to-end neural inference without hard ontology coupling.

question: In whole slide image classification, how do different approaches address the trade-off between compact feature aggregation and preservation of diagnostically relevant morphological detail?
answer: FOCUS addresses this trade-off by introducing knowledge-enhanced adaptive visual compression that selectively retains discriminative regions while compressing background and redundant context—demonstrated through superior few-shot performance over SOTA MIL methods (TransMIL, DS-MIL, DTFD-MIL, WiKG-MIL, TOP-MIL, ViLa-MIL) and strong pooling baselines (Max, Mean, Attentive Pooling with CONCH) on TCGA-NSCLC, CAMELYON, and UBC-OCEAN under 4-, 8-, and 16-shot settings (FOCUS). In contrast, Flow-MIL tackles the same trade-off by replacing conventional aggregation with a normalizing flow-based latent space construction that explicitly preserves information during feature summarization—motivated by the observation that standard methods inevitably discard subtle morphological patterns essential for diagnosis (Flow-MIL). The paper GMMamba: Group Masking Mamba for Whole Slide Image Classification points out that previous approaches to reducing redundancy primarily focused on data dropping and similarity replacement; data dropping randomly discards a proportion of the data, while similarity replacement employs distance metrics and clustering to replace similar data with representative centers. Both methods risk discarding crucial details, potentially undermining accuracy and stability. The paper M3amba: Memory Mamba is All You Need for Whole Slide Image Classification points out that M3amba achieves competitive performance across all metrics, outperforming attention-based methods ACMIL and MHIM-ABMIL by 6.2%, 7.0%, and 3.8% in accuracy, respectively, and significantly reduces computational complexity and model parameters compared to transformer-based methods MHIM-TransMIL and TransMIL while maintaining remarkable classification performance, benefiting from efficient long-range modeling.

question: In weakly-supervised video anomaly detection, how do different approaches formulate temporal saliency or activation refinement to improve the localization of anomalous snippets?
answer: Paper A (CMHKF) formulates extended temporal saliency by aggregating saliency scores across neighboring frames within a fixed window: specifically, for frame n, the extended saliency is defined as $\tilde{S}_a^{(n)} = \begin{cases} S_a^{(j)} + S_a^{(n)}, & \text{if } \exists j \in K \text{ and } n \in R_j \\ S_a^{(n)}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$, where $R_j = [\max(1, a_j - w), \min(a_j + w, N)]$ defines the temporal support region around anchor frame $a_j$ with window size $w$. This explicitly enhances saliency through neighborhood-aware additive fusion.
